news.title: Trump's Support Erodes in GOP Strongholds Ahead of Midterms
news.text: President Trump is losing ground even in territory that should be friendliest to him. New polling shows his approval rating has turned negative in 11 states he carried comfortably in the 2024 election, a warning sign for Republicans as they head into November's midterms. As of July 30, Trump's approval sits at 36 percent nationally, while 59 percent disapprove of his performance, putting his net approval at a steep negative 24 points, according to Newsweek's report on Civiqs' ongoing online tracking poll. That poll draws from registered voters and has collected more than 120,000 responses since Trump returned to office on January 20, 2025. Red States Turning ColdWhat makes this trend notable isn't just the national number, it's where the softening is happening. When Trump took office for his second term back in January 2025, his approval rating was positive in every single state he had won by 10 points or more in the 2024 race against Kamala Harris. That's no longer true. At least 11 of those states have since flipped into negative territory. The timing offers some clues about what's driving the shift. In several states, Trump's numbers turned negative around the time he announced tariffs on U.S. trading partners back in April. In others, including Kentucky and Missouri, the drop lines up with his announcement of a war with Iran in February. Where the Numbers Stand NowAlaska shows the steepest decline among the group, with a net approval of negative 14, reflecting 40 percent approval against 54 percent disapproval. Iowa sits at the same negative 14 mark, with 44 percent approving and 49 percent disapproving. Texas and Ohio both come in at negative 13. In Texas, 40 percent approve of Trump while 54 percent disapprove. Ohio shows a similar split, with 40 percent approval and 53 percent disapproval. Florida follows closely behind at negative 12, with 42 percent approval and 54 percent disapproval. South Carolina sits at negative 9, with 42 percent approving and 51 percent disapproving. Missouri comes in at negative 7, with 44 percent approval and 51 percent disapproval. Louisiana stands at negative 4, with 45 percent approving and 49 percent disapproving. Kentucky and Nebraska are both at negative 3. Kentucky shows 39 percent approval against 53 percent disapproval, while Nebraska shows 45 percent approval against 48 percent disapproval. Mississippi has the narrowest gap of the group, sitting at just negative 1, with 47 percent approving and 48 percent disapproving. Even His Strongest States Aren't ImmuneThe softening isn't limited to states now underwater. Even in the places where Trump remains most popular, the trend line is heading in the wrong direction. Wyoming, his strongest state, started his second term with a net approval of positive 45. That figure has since fallen to positive 19. North Dakota tells a similar story, dropping from positive 31 down to positive 19 over the same stretch. Why This Matters for NovemberThese shifts carry real political weight heading into the midterms. Control of Congress hangs in the balance, and Republicans are working to hold onto narrow majorities in both the House and Senate for the rest of Trump's term. Even modest changes in voter sentiment, especially in states that have historically leaned Republican, could end up shaping how competitive individual races become this fall.
news.summary: President Trump's approval rating has turned negative in 11 states he won by at least 10 points in 2024, including Florida, Ohio and Texas, according to a Civiqs poll.
news.author: Sagar Kar

news.title: Pete Buttigieg, AOC and Jon Ossoff poll ahead of Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris for White House run
news.text:
Three Democratic heavyweights are now polling ahead of both California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris in the increasingly crowded race for the party’s 2028 presidential nomination, according to a new survey.

A hypothetical Democratic primary poll conducted by The Public Sentiment Institute between July 25 and July 29 among 762 likely Michigan voters found former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg leading the pack with 24.2% support.

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff followed at 13.9%, while New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez came in third with 10.7%.

That left Newsom in fourth place at 10%, narrowly behind Ocasio-Cortez, while Harris trailed the field with just 5.1%.

The Michigan results mark a striking contrast to earlier national polling, where Harris and Newsom had largely occupied the top two spots among Democratic hopefuls.

A national Center Square Voters’ Voice Poll released in June found Harris leading the field with 27% support, nearly double Newsom’s 14%. Buttigieg placed third at 11%, while Ocasio-Cortez registered 8%.

That survey also showed both California Democrats slipping from earlier polling. Harris fell from 33% in October and 31% in March to 27%, while Newsom dropped from 21% to 14%, suggesting the race was beginning to open up.

Another national Emerson College Polling survey released in May painted a less favorable picture for both Californians. 

Newsom led that poll with 16%, but Harris managed only 10%, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also reached double digits and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear climbed to 9%, signaling a broader field of contenders beginning to gain traction.

Despite their weaker showing in the Michigan survey, betting markets continue to view Newsom as one of the Democrats’ strongest potential nominees.

As of Sunday, prediction market Polymarket gave Newsom the highest odds of winning the Democratic nomination at 19%. Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff stood at 15% and14% respectively, followed by Harris at 9%. 

Kalshi’s market painted a similar picture, placing Newsom at 18%, Ossoff at 15%, Ocasio-Cortez at 14%, and Harris at 9.5%. 

Several of the potential candidates have publicly addressed speculation about 2028.

Harris, who has made appearances in early-voting states including Michigan and South Carolina, told Rev. Al Sharpton in April she was considering another White House bid.

“I might. I am thinking about it.”

She added: “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office. I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.”

Newsom acknowledged last year that a presidential campaign remained a possibility.

“I’m not thinking about running, but it’s a path that I could see unfold,” he told The Wall Street Journal in June 2025.

Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, has downplayed the idea of a White House campaign.

“My ambition is to change this country,” she said during a conversation with former Obama adviser David Axelrod.

“Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever.

“A living wage is forever, workers’ rights are forever, women’s rights, all of that, and so anyways…to a finer point to your question is that when you aren’t attached, when you haven’t been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating.”

Ossoff has been even more direct, telling CNN he has no plans to seek the presidency.

“I am not running for president in 2028, I have no interest in running for president in 2028.”

The Georgia senator added that he is “laser-focused” on winning reelection this year.

Other candidates in the poll included Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who received 3.8%, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who drew 3.6%. More than one in five voters — 21.7% — remained undecided, underscoring how unsettled the Democratic field remains more than two years before the election.

news.summary: A Michigan survey shows Pete Buttigieg, Jon Ossoff and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ahead of the California governor and former vice president in a hypothetical Democratic primary.
news.author: Zain Khan

news.title: Ex-‘60 Minutes’ boss Bill Owens wants to launch rival news show with Scott Pelley, other fired staffers: sources
news.text:
A former boss of “60 Minutes” wants to launch a rival news series with Scott Pelley and other correspondents and producers who have recently exited the iconic show — but insiders are skeptical about whether it can get off the ground, The Post has learned. 

Bill Owens – who resigned last year as “60 Minutes” executive producer amid a dustup between CBS and President Trump over how a Kamala Harris interview was edited – is looking to raise around $50 million to fund two years’ worth of in-depth and investigative news segments, sources with knowledge said.

The lump sum Owens is seeking would bankroll everything from staffing and production to marketing and legal, sources added. Still, for the idea to work, former “60 Minutes” journalists would likely be forced to take a drastic pay cut.

“I think they’re asking for too much money,” a source familar with the plan said. “They’re looking at the old ’60 Minutes’ model and they’re all used to mega salaries.”

A source close to Owens denied the plans.

Still, some insiders speculated that a “60 Minutes”-style venture could potentially capitalize on recent upheaval at the 57-year-old show after CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss cleaned house in recent months.

A second source said Owens is angling to enlist the bombastic Pelley, who was fired in June after he tore into Weiss, claiming she was “murdering ‘60 Minutes” during a staff meeting.

Indeed, there has been chatter that Pelley’s scorched-earth exit – in which he also slammed the show’s new executive producer Bilton, telling him he’d “never be welcomed” – was partly a ploy to gin up buzz ahead of an upcoming venture.

Owens could also tap other fired “60 Minutes” staffers including ex-correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, former executive producer Tanya Simon and senior producers Guy Campanile and Draggan Mihailovich and Matthew Polevoy, a source with knowledge said.

Owens declined to comment. Other former “60 Minutes” staffers couldn’t be reached for comment.

As The Post reported last week, the show’s new executive producer Nick Bilton has struggled to hire senior producers and has used interviews with prospective candidates as “therapy sessions” to vent about his own work conditions.

Last week, Bilton announced four “new faces” coming to “60 Minutes” — Ross Douthat, Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni and Trevor Phillips, as well as longtime CBS News journo Norah O’Donnell. Some of the hires have been met with skepticism over their broadcast TV qualifications.

Owens shopped the idea of a rival show earlier this year, but hit some snags — including securing money and a platform, sources close to the situation said.

In recent weeks, however, fired “60 Minutes” staffers have put together a business plan and pitch deck. The old gang is hoping to produce a documentary-style program for streaming and potentially digital platforms, according to sources.

“Rather than a chat show, it will be deeply reported, similar to ‘60 Minutes’,” a source said.

Still, Owens and his colleagues face a major problem — namely the stiff costs of producing a “60 Minutes”-type program and the challenge of convincing deep-pocketed streamers like Netflix, Apple and YouTube — or even a TV network like NBC — to foot the bill.

“There isn’t a huge appetite,” from major streaming platforms or broadcast networks, said one TV agent.

Insiders have speculated that a prime target for the series would be Netflix, the prospective archrival to CBS owner Paramount Skydance and its pending, $110 billion merger partner Warner Bros Discovery, the owner of HBO Max.

“There’s no clamoring on the Netflix side for overall news,” said one former streaming exec. “But for a tightly done show that isn’t too expensive, maybe it could work.”

Pivot podcast co-host Scott Galloway has been vocal on his show about why Netflix should hire Pelley and other former “60 Minutes” to create their own version, citing the show’s success.

“If I were [Netflix CEO] Ted Sarandos, I would call Scott Pelley and Anderson Cooper, pay them $10 million each, you hire whoever the f you want, including an executive producer and Netflix will put something out called. ‘The Hour,'” he said recently.

If Owens isn’t able to ink a hefty deal with a streamer, he will need to prepare to make his show on a shoestring budget, said one source who works in the digital video space. Building an audience of subscribers — a notoriously difficult prospect — would be also vital to success, the person added. 

On YouTube, a video with 1 million views typically earns around $5,000 in advertising revenue. One million subscribers can bring in upwards of $1 million a year, and sponsorships can meaningfully increase that amount depending on the sponsor. 

Owens’ efforts come as Weiss has decimated the show’s staff in a bid to update the program and address criticisms that it was marred by left-wing bias.

Pelley had griped that his bosses were trying to interfere with his reports and insert “political bias.” CBS News denied Pelley’s claims and said the edits were part of the normal journalistic process between correspondent and editor.

Although Owens quit “60 Minutes” last year – before Weiss’ arrival – he too complained about interference from higher ups.

The exec quit the lofty gig last year when the show’s parent company Paramount was settling a lawsuit against President Trump over claims of “deceptive editing” of an interview with Harris that aired days before the November 2024 presidential election.

As previously reported by The Post, Bilton has been stewing over how he was treated by Pelley and the staff, who applauded the correspondent for standing up to the new boss.

John Fetterman is a little less lonely these days, but not because his courage has proven contagious to Democratic elders.

The Pennsylvania progressive has been branded a Benedict Arnold for speaking the truth about the ascendant, anti-civilizational forces within his own party

Bernie Sanders “keeps pushing these communists and these . . . awful anti-American people,” Fetterman argued last month after the collapse of Graham Platner’s candidacy in Maine.

His “anti-American” modifier was of special import because it cut to the core of the conflict.

The Democrats’ bloody civil war isn’t about health care, or immigration, or LGBT issues, or marginal tax rates.

It’s about two irreconcilable worldviews: one that celebrates the United States as exceptionally commendable, and the other that scorns it as exceptionally reprehensible — often using Israel as a proxy. 

In Michigan, a pair of lawmakers are at last acknowledging this hard, inconvenient truth. 

Rep. Haley Stevens, the establishment pick to represent the Democrats in the Great Lakes State’s Senate race, has taken the gloves off against Abdul El-Sayed, the short-tempered, Jew-baiting Hasan Piker fanboy who boasts a double-digit polling lead ahead of Tuesday’s primary.

“Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens posited in a scorching tweet Thursday.

Rep. Hillary Scholten, a Stevens supporter and her colleague in Michigan’s House delegation, went even further, expressing doubt that she’d back El-Sayed if he prevails Aug. 4.

“I will not stand beside someone who has allowed distinctly anti-American sentiment to enter our public dialogue,” said Scholten, citing El-Sayed’s decision to campaign alongside Piker, he of “America deserved 9/11” infamy.

It’s heartening to see some Democrats, any Democrats, join Fetterman’s camp.

Where’s everyone else?

Stevens is desperate and highly motivated; Scholten is an anonymous congresswoman.

It’s to their credit that they’re speaking out, but neither has the power to turn their party’s ship around.

And those who might be able to move the needle remain unwilling to do so.

Take former President Barack Obama.

He has a policy of staying above the primary-election fray, but Obama has never shied away from advising Democrats on what course to take at a pivotal moment — remember his crusade against Peak Woke?

Instead of pushing back against the anti-American revanchists, though, Obama has signaled his support for them by sanitizing the radicalism and praising the tactics of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Perhaps it should come as no surprise that the apology-tour president who spent the weeks after Oct. 7 setting the stage for the blood libels to come won’t stand in the breach; he shares too many common convictions with the radicals.

The same cannot be said of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who has described himself as a guardian of the Jewish people and opposed Obama’s concession-filled Iran nuclear deal.

No one could mistake Schumer for Ronald Reagan, but he’s historically stood up for his country and the relatively just, peaceful and prosperous world order it upholds.

Which is what makes his listless response to his party’s descent into the unpatriotic fever swamp so dispiriting.

Sure, Schumer is supporting Stevens now, just as he threw his weight behind Gov. Janet Mills’ doomed campaign against Platner.

But in both races, his boilerplate endorsement statements and cash haven’t cut it.

Voters are hungry for authenticity and confidence.

The anti-American faction has no difficulty projecting both: They are open about their disdain of this country, and secure in their belief that fair is foul and foul is fair.

Schumer, on the other hand, has refrained from honestly speaking the truth about them — much less refusing them support in general elections.

Why should anyone take his endorsement of Stevens seriously after seeing how he bent like a cheap folding chair for Platner?

The minority leader is desperate to be majority leader, and El-Sayed is the favorite to represent Democrats on the ballot in November.

So mum’s the word. 

He’s also likely calculated that letting loose on El-Sayed would prove fruitless after the establishment’s stinging losses in Maine and New York City.

He feels impotent, because at this point he is.

Throwing money at the problem this late in the game is no substitute for showing moral clarity at the first whiff of these noxious ideas and hateful people.

And if you’re expecting prospective 2028 front-runners like California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris to push back come campaign season, don’t.

They’re soulless, finger-to-the-wind followers interested only in what’s best for their careers.

Obama’s content, Schumer’s craven, and the rest of them just don’t care enough to fight the good fight.

These spineless weaklings have, for their various reasons, picked the path of least resistance over that of the righteous.

But they have underestimated the long-term cost of that calculation.

Because the party they’ll be left with will be not misguided, but morally repugnant.

news.title: Nearly three-quarters of MAGA voters would back candidate accused of domestic violence: poll
news.text:
Nearly three-quarters of MAGA voters would back a candidate accused of domestic violence, and two-thirds would stick with one accused of sexual assault, according to recent polling.

More broadly, most self-identified MAGA Donald Trump voters surveyed by Politico said they would stand by a GOP candidate mired in any of 12 separate scandals, including a past DUI conviction, accepting gifts from lobbyists and concealing a terminal illness.

By contrast, voters who identified as having supported Kamala Harris in 2024 were significantly less willing to indulge damaged reputations — with two notable exceptions.

The findings suggest that, for many voters, scandal is less a disqualifier than background noise, with President Trump remaining the most durable illustration of this phenomenon. He weathered political isolation after the January 6 Capitol riot, four criminal indictments and a seemingly endless catalogue of controversies so far in his second term.

"Scandal doesn't mean what it did 15 years ago. The rules have changed, and Republican voters know it," GOP strategist Ford O'Connell told Politico. "Republicans, particularly MAGA voters, have learned that Queensberry rules don't win in modern politics. Today it's a full-contact fight, more UFC than civics class, and anything goes."

The poll — conducted July 13-15 with 2,061 U.S. adults — asked voters whether they would stick with their party's candidate through 12 different scandals if the midterm elections were held tomorrow.

MAGA voters were most forgiving of candidates who used legal tax loopholes, with 82 percent saying they would still back them. Large shares also said they would support candidates who had been convicted of a DUI (76 percent), accepted gifts from lobbyists (75 percent) or been photographed wearing blackface (74 percent).

Support remained strong, though it dipped somewhat, when voters were asked about more serious allegations: 72 percent said they would back a candidate accused of domestic violence, and 66 percent said the same about one accused of sexual assault.

The smallest shares — though still majorities — said they would stand by candidates who made antisemitic comments (58 percent) or shared classified information with a foreign government (57 percent).

Harris voters, meanwhile, were more generally more circumspect, with less than half saying they'd throw their support behind a Democratic candidate entangled in six of 12 scandals.

About 40 percent said they would stand by candidates accused of domestic violence or sexual assault, or those who had accepted gifts from lobbyists.

But when it came to two scandals, Harris voters were slightly more forgiving than Trump voters. Seventy percent said they would back a candidate previously convicted of a DUI, compared with 65 percent of MAGA voters. And about half said they would support an individual who made antisemitic comments — 2 percent more than MAGA voters.

Far from being in the realm of the hypothetical, several of these scandals have played a prominent role in races across the country this year.

For instance, Graham Platner, who was the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Maine, was accused last month by a former girlfriend of sexual assault, following a string of other controversies. After losing the backing of key Democratic allies seemingly overnight, Platner dropped out of the race while denying the allegations.

Ohio Rep. Max Miller, who is running for re-election, has also been accused by his ex-wife of abuse, including allegations that he held a gun to her head and broke her daughter's collarbone. Miller has denied the allegations and is suing his ex-wife.

On a livestream Sunday, Miller said, "I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November."

That same day, his former father-in-law, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, issued a statement saying Miller should resign and seek mental health treatment.

"He is a danger to my daughter," Moreno said. "If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them."

And so I think trying to figure out, it seems pretty reasonable to want to be able to shut down an A.I. system if it's doing things we don't want to. Can we already do that? And if not, how do we get there?

STEPHANOPOULOS: Is it going to take a more serious crisis to get the kind of regulation we need?

TONER: I really hope not. I mean, I'll be honest with you, a lot of people in the A.I. safety space and A.I. governance space think that the political will is just not there right now. And they worry that we need some kind of Chernobyl accident, some kind of real-world disaster to wake up and to actually take action.

One thing that gives me hope is seeing the level of concern that incidents like this OpenAI incident from a couple weeks ago produce. I think it's right for that to be worrying for us. And if we can be sufficiently activated, sufficiently energized by incidents like this, where thankfully no one was hurt, then maybe we can get there without needing something more serious to happen.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Helen Toner, thanks for your time this morning.

Coming up, just over three months to the midterms, we're in Michigan for the key Senate primary that could decide control of the Senate.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

GOV. GRETCHEN WHITMER, (D) MICHIGAN: Just like me, Haley will do whatever it takes to get things done for the people of Michigan. And we need her now more than ever.

SEN. ELIABETH WARREN, (D) MASSACHUSETTS: Abdul is the only candidate in this race who can build the grassroots movement needed to win in November.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Key endorsements in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary for progressive Abdul El-Sayed and moderate Congresswoman Haley Stevens.

So, can Democrats hold on to the seat in November? Our report from Michigan when we come back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

STEPHANOPOULOS: The Michigan Senate race is a must-hold seat for Democrats, and our political director, Averi Harper, traveled to the state where a fierce battle between moderates and progressives is playing out ahead of the primary this Tuesday.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

AVERI HARPER, ABC NEWS POLITICAL DIRECTOR (voice-over): Here in Michigan, Democrats are fighting for the future of their party.

FELECIA HARDAWAY, MICHIGAN VOTER: I just want to see us as Democrats be stronger. I want somebody who can win for us.

HARPER (voice-over): Progressive former public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and moderate Congresswoman Haley Stevens are locked in a tight race to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

El-Sayed racking up the support of the party's biggest progressives.

REP. ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ, (D) NEW YORK: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and I may come from different places, but we're forged from the same fight.

SEN. BERNIE SANDERS, (I) VERMONT: Please welcome the next United States Senator from the state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed.

HARPER (voice-over): As establishment Democrats have thrown their weight behind Stevens, including the senator they're both running to replace.

SEN. GARY PETERS, (D) MICHIGAN: I think Haley Stevens is an outstanding candidate, and she's going to make a great senator, particularly like the fact that she's kind of a practical, common-sense person who tries to find common ground. And, God, we need to find common ground.

HARPER (voice-over): El-Sayed and Stevens are competing to face off against former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in November. For Democrats to have a chance to take back control of the Senate, they must hold this seat in Michigan.

ABDUL EL-SAYED, (D) MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE: I'm the best candidate to take on Mike Rogers and beat him.

REP. HALEY STEVENS, (D) MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE: I'm capturing all this enthusiasm I see everywhere across my state.

HARPER (voice-over): The two went head-to-head in their final debate earlier this week, where support for Israel and AIPAC spending, a flashpoint in the race, was front and center.

EL-SAYED: Just last week, our friend here voted to send $3.3 billion of your tax dollars to a foreign government. That is the pro quo that comes with a quid of $30 million spent by AIPAC.

STEVENS: I don't think there's much difference between super PACs going in for Abdul or super PACs going in for me. We have a problem with campaign finance reform in this country.

HARPER (voice-over): We caught up with El-Sayed at a campaign stop on Detroit's East Side.

(CROWD CHANTING)

HARPER (voice-over): El-Sayed has centered his campaign on getting corporate money out of politics and pushing for universal healthcare.

EL-SAYED: I can win back the voters we lost in 2024, and I can build a coalition that includes young people who actually want to be in the politics again. So if you're doing the math and you're watching this campaign and you're looking at who you want to be on that debate stage with Mike Rogers, I think there's one answer.

HARPER: Strong Black community here on the East Side of Detroit. Can you talk about the perception that some people may have left over from 2024 that you did not fully support Kamala Harris? And do you worry that that could hurt you with a key voting bloc here in the state of Michigan?

EL-SAYED: Well, you saw the coalition that we're building. I was proud to endorse Vice President Harris on day one. Now, I deeply disagreed with her position on the genocide in Gaza. But I endorsed her. A vote is about the future, not the past.

HARPER (voice-over): Just south of Detroit, Stevens is campaigning on a moderate message she hopes will win over independent voters as concern among national Democrats grows that El-Sayed can't win in the fall.

STEVENS: I'm campaigning in the underdog way that I, you know, have approached all of my races to win for the people.

HARPER (voice-over): That approach and her delivery leading to this viral clip.

STEVENS: And you better believe I'm going to be doing it with a little bit of joy, a little bit of enthusiasm, a little bit of energy, and a little bit of stick it to them because that's the Michigan way.

HARPER (voice-over): Stevens making clear where she stands on Israel compared to her opponent.

STEVENS: He wants a one-state solution. That's not going to bring us anywhere closer to peace. I want to see a two-state solution where the people of Israel and the people of Palestine are living together side by side.

HARPER: And you've received millions of dollars in support from some political action committees. How do you convince voters that the folks who are cutting those checks are not influencing you?

STEVENS: Well, look, my motivation for everything I do in public service, from the time when I worked on that U.S. auto rescue and the administration of the great Barack Obama, to when I first put up my hand to run for Congress to flip a seat, through my years serving Michigan and delivering for Michigan -- Michigan has been my North Star. The only thing influencing my vote is the people of Michigan.

HARPER (voice-over): Stevens' supporters pointing to her experience.

JACQUELINE VANDERGRIFT, MICHIGAN VOTER: Haley Stevens is a fighter.

LINDA WITHER, MICHIGAN VOTER: Her push, her work, her drive, she doesn't give up.

HARPER (voice-over): But back in Detroit, we met voters excited about El-Sayed.

OSCAR RIDLEY, MICHIGAN VOTER: He's actually -- looks like he's willing to work for the people.

HARPER: What do you say to Democrats who think that Abdul El-Sayed wouldn't be able to win in a general election?

GEOFFREY MARTIN, MICHIGAN VOTER: Yeah, I would say look at Trump, because people said that about him too.

HARPER (voice-over): For "This Week," Averi Harper, ABC News, Detroit.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

STEPHANOPOULOS: Thanks, Averi, for that.

We'll go back to the Roundtable for their take on the midterms when we come back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

REP. HAKEEM JEFFRIES, (D) HOUSE MINORITY LEADER: We have just 100 days until the midterm elections. 100 days to change direction in this country. This is no longer a marathon, it's a sprint.

REP. MIKE JOHNSON, (R-LA) HOUSE SPEAKER: We continue to deliver for the people, and we're going to continue that streak all the way through the end of this year and into the next Congress. We're increasingly confident that we will hold and grow this majority in the House.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

STEPHANOPOULOS: Which one of those men will be Speaker? That's what is at stake in the midterms. We're back with the Roundtable.

Doug, I want to start with you. What's your sense of where things stand right now?

But, and there's a really big but there, when I was Commerce Director for the Republican National Committee in 2010, our magic number for Obama was 46. We felt if he is --

(CROSSTALK)

STEPHANOPOULOS: And his approval.

HEYE: Approval. We thought if he was at or below that, we'd take back the House. And every poll in the run-up had him at 44, 45, 46. Trump is nowhere near that, but the map is so ridiculously different because of the redistricting on the Republican side and on the Democratic side. It is a dramatically different playing field.

So when I see Democrats talking about waves and picking up 40 seats, that's not based in real life.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Let's pick up on Doug's point, Michelle. No one knows what the magic number is anymore, but we did see three serious national polls this week, all showing President Trump under 35 percent, which is about as low as you can go. It's reaching Richard Nixon territory.

COTTLE: It is continuing to sink, which should make his party extremely nervous. This is why they've been working to rig the game, redistricting, he's trying to play with states' voting systems, that sort of thing. That said, I do think that Doug is right. And there's still an opportunity for them if they play their cards right, maybe to pick up three or four more seats.

The problem right now, George, is that the Democratic Party must define itself and make sure that we don't get caught in this socialist wave, which is, you know, popping up here, there and everywhere. But I think Michigan is going to tell us a lot about this current electorate. We know they're angry, they want change. And both candidates are trying not to allow the labels to define them.

Miss Stevens said I'm not a moderate, I'm a populist. Mr. Abdul said I'm not a progressive, I'm a populist. They want to capture this anger and they want to see if they can ride it to the polls.

STEPHANOPOULOS: You've been a Democratic insurgent, you've been part of the Democratic --

BRAZILE: Establishment.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Establishment. So when you look at Michigan right now, how concerned are you that a lot of establishment Democrats believe that El-Sayed cannot win in November?

BRAZILE: Well, that young man at the end said, well, Trump won. It's going to be difficult. He will have to unite the party. He's going to have to bring the establishment wing back on board to his side. And he's going to have to, I think, do a better job of messaging for the fall in order to win swing voters. Michigan is a purple state. It's going to be tough.

STEPHANOPOULOS: It does appear, Chris Christie, that the Democrats could hurt themselves, but that a lot of the Republicans are going to have to go into this election without really the help of Donald Trump.

CHRISTIE: Thank God. For most of them they don't want that help. They're going to be treating him like he's, you know, got malaria by the time we get to October.

STEPHANOPOULOS: He's having this convention in September.

CHRISTIE: Yes, that's going to -- that's going to be a problem for a lot of Republicans who are going to feel like they need to be there because he's going to be taking attendance. But you could be sure, you know, Doug was talking to us earlier about having cameras in places when you're doing op research for a party, you can be sure that Democrats will be having as much of that video as they can for those people.

To me, George, the key number in the polls you talked about, yes, the 30s are bad, but here's the one that I look at for a midterm. The president right now is minus 45 among independents, and so in these races that are going to be very close, those independents are going to make the difference. Minus 45 is something I can't even conceive of. You know, this is a guy who has won independence in the past.

He in the Quinnipiac Poll was 22 percent approval among independents, 22-67. Also, I want to find the eleven percent of independents who have no opinion on Donald Trump. Those people are probably comatose at this point to not have an opinion one way or the other. So when you're looking at this like, let's look at Mike Lawler in --

STEPHANOPOULOS: Here in New York.

CHRISTIE: Here in New York, where Tom Kean, Jr. in a suburban district in New Jersey, in the northeast, if you're looking at a minus 45 of the leader of your party among independents, you're going to be running as far away from him as you possibly can to try to save your own skin. And that's going to place the president in a position where he is going to be angry, even angrier than he is now, when those people are saying, no, thank you, I'd prefer not to have you visit.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Doug, that's one issue. The other issue is that the enthusiasm gap we are seeing right now between Democrats and Republicans. Democrats appear more motivated to vote, and we saw something pretty remarkable over the week. I want to show it up on the screen. It was a post from former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene.

You see her there with Thomas Massie, Marjorie Taylor Greene at Tucker Carlson's house, and they're saying the movement has begun. And so you're seeing a little bit of a crack up in the MAGA movement as you're heading into the midterms.

HEYE: Well, I think there's been a crack up within the Republican Party for a long time, and it actually predates --

STEPHANOPOULOS: And Trump exploited that back in '16.

HEYE: He exploited it. But it existed before him. And it's why I would tell Democrats, be very careful of who you're going to nominate, because we can do a litany of the Republican candidates who are on the road side of political roadkill, from Todd Akin and Richard Murdaugh to Mark Robinson and Doug Mastriano in the last cycle.

When you nominate people who can't win, you're exposing the divides within your own party and the other side is there to exploit it. And Republicans know that they have opportunities based on who Democrats are nominating. Be careful and learn the lesson that Republicans have shown you over and over and over.

(CROSSTALK)

COTTLE: George, to speak to Governor Christie's point about the Independents, when it comes general election time, this fire on the Democratic left has got to translate into a candidate that can win over these Independents who are unhappy with Donald Trump.

And if you have a bunch of candidates who are too far to the left, that's going to completely hurt the Democratic advantage.

STEPHANOPOULOS: Donna, I want to put that to you, but let me first put up on the screen, which we're going to be seeing a lot of, I think, from the Republicans, and that's the DSA platform, the Democratic Socialist America platform, defund the police, abolish ICE, defund the Department of Defense, abolish the Senate.

What do Democrats do with that?

BRAZILE: Put that in trash. I mean, even the candidate running for governor, the Socialist candidate in Wisconsin, she's changing her position on all those issues, defund the police, defund the Pentagon. I'm like, what the hell are you going to have left standing?

Look, we talk about what's going on with the left, the right. All of the election deniers in Arizona, the primary that we just saw, I mean, the right is still trying to push out the establishment in the Republican Party. So both political parties are dealing with this insurgency.

But I have to say one piece of good news. When you look at some of these candidates, the senatorial and gubernatorial, they're outperforming where Kamala Harris was just a couple of years ago.

STEPHANOPOULOS: We only have about 30 seconds. Let me just go around the table quickly.

Who has control of the House? Who has control of the Senate in December?

HEYE: Democrats control the House. Senate? I have no idea, George.

CHRISTIE: I think Democrats control the House. And on the Senate side, I think the Republicans, it's 50/50. J.D. Vance is going to spend a lot of time in the chair.

BRAZILE: I don't want to agree with Chris. I agree.

COTTLE: I'll throw in with him.

STEPHANOPOULOS: OK. We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

STEPHANOPOULOS: That is all for us today. Thanks for sharing part of your Sunday with us. Check out "World News Tonight" and I'll see you tomorrow on GMA.

news.title: The pro-Israel lobby has swayed US presidents  since Truman. It must end with Trump | Ian Lustick and Eli Clifton
news.text:
In 1948, with war raging in Palestine, Harry Truman found himself trapped.

On one side were Zionist lobbyists and the president’s domestic political advisers, who were urging him to support the establishment of a Jewish state in as much of Palestine as possible. On the other were his top foreign policy and national security officials, led by the secretary of state, George C Marshall. Their unanimous recommendation was to prevent the establishment of a Jewish state, which they believed would trigger war in the Middle East and endanger the future of US relations with the Arab and Muslim world.

With the exception perhaps of George Washington, no diplomatic or military leader in American history had a reputation for patriotic virtue and skilled devotion to duty comparable to that of Marshall. Truman was in awe of the secretary of state, who, as chief of staff of the US armed forces, had been hailed by Winston Churchill as “the true organizer of victory” in the second world war. After the war, it had been Marshall who launched the plan named after him to rebuild Europe.

In the mid-1940s, Marshall pushed quietly but steadily against the Zionist movement’s proposals to establish a Jewish state in Palestine. He was concerned that American support would open opportunities for the Soviet Union to exploit Arab anger, put Middle Eastern oil supplies at risk in the event of a war between the Soviet Union and the United States, and require the deployment of unavailable American troops to prevent bloodshed and instability in Palestine. These were, indeed, the strongly held views of virtually all of Truman’s most important military and foreign policy advisers.

Truman was personally and deeply moved by the suffering of Jewish survivors of the Nazi “Final Solution”, but also irritated by and at times furious with the constant hectoring to which he was subjected by campaigners for recognition of a Jewish state in Palestine, including the World Zionist Organization and a host of other Jewish delegations, friends and politicians. Despite his personal exasperation, he could not ignore them. Coming in an election year that would pit him against Governor Thomas Dewey of New York, pressures from the Zionist lobby forced him into an excruciating and embarrassing position.

With Palestine engulfed by civil war, Arab states threatening to invade and the last British soldiers about to leave the country, Truman called a meeting of his top advisers on 12 May 1948. According to Marshall’s own account of the meeting, he warned Truman against adopting the policy strongly advanced by Clark Clifford, his main political adviser, to recognize the state of Israel before it was established.

Such a move, according to Marshall, would be a “transparent dodge to win a few votes”, he said, leaving the “great dignity of the office of the President … seriously diminished”. Marshall declared he would not personally be able to vote for Truman should he bow to political pressure on the issue. A shaken Truman closed the meeting by saying he agreed with Marshall.

However, within two days, exquisitely sensitive to the tenuousness of his hold on the presidency and the power of Zionist sympathizers to throw New York’s electoral votes to the Republicans, he ordered that the US recognize Israel.

Today, the influence of the groups loosely known as the Israel lobby has only become more powerful. Truman’s bind – caught between his sense of the national interest and the domestic political price of defying a powerful lobby – was something that, in the decades to come, president after president would experience.

To fast forward: Donald Trump’s decision to go to war on Iran earlier this year came after a sustained campaign by Israel to convince the US to join the disastrous operation. It also came in defiance of several of his top advisers, as well as the 45% of Republicans who hold an unfavorable view of Israel. That decision may be most quickly explained as yet another example of the erratic policymaking that define Trump’s two terms as president. But a closer examination of the experience of several of his predecessors reveals that this presidential decision is more the rule than the exception.

The fact is that from Truman to Trump, most American presidents have caved to the demands of Israel and its advocates. Driven by the fear of domestic political defeats, presidents have regularly rejected or abandoned foreign policies that both they and their most senior advisers believed were in the best interests of the US and at the expense of making meaningful progress in bringing a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Our new book, Israel’s Lobby, tracks the growth over decades of the most powerful foreign policy lobby in American history. Comprised of a panoply of organizations, groups and individuals who advocate American policies that explicitly favor the interests of Israel, the lobby was nurtured – and has been encouraged and guided – by Israeli governments. Exploiting the fact that most voters were ignorant or uncaring on the issue, the lobby used enormous resources and concentrated attention to punish or reward politicians at every level depending on their willingness to follow lobby instructions.

Over 20 years after the Truman episode, for example, President Gerald Ford launched what he referred to as a “reassessment” of US policy in the Middle East. The initiative had been advanced by Ford and his secretary of state, Henry Kissinger, as a way to escape from two years of embarrassing failures to move toward a comprehensive Arab-Israeli peace agreement. Both Ford and Kissinger had become intensely dissatisfied with Israeli stonewalling.

The reassessment was conducted by the committee of “Wise Men” convened by Kissinger: former government officials who had served as pillars of the postwar US foreign policy establishment. The unanimous recommendation of the committee was pressure on Israel to withdraw from the West Bank and Gaza Strip in order to achieve a comprehensive peace, in cooperation with the Soviet Union.

Clear indications that Ford intended to accept this recommendation triggered a powerful mobilization by leading Israel lobby organizations, such as the Conference of Presidents of Major Jewish Organizations and the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). The lobby’s decisive achievement was a letter drafted by Aipac and delivered to Ford demanding that the president “make it clear … that the United States, acting in its own national interests, stands firmly with Israel in the search for peace in future negotiations”, signed by 76 senators.

Ford was “mad as hell” at what he believed to be an Israeli campaign to use the lobby to obstruct diplomacy. But he was cowed. To protect his chances for election the following year, Ford rejected the unanimous recommendation from the “Wise Men”, returning instead to the step-by-step process that had so infuriated him, a process of essentially buying slices of the Sinai Peninsula – seized from Egypt in 1967 – from Israel with increasing amounts of aid and then returning them to Egypt. Ford and Kissinger also vastly increased the scale and scope of US support for Israel.

That included a sweeping new collection of US political, economic, military and diplomatic commitments made in a US-Israeli Memorandum of Agreement that, along with secret annexes, was signed on 1 September 1975. Aides to Kissinger described the guarantees and concessions made to Israel in these negotiations as “mind-boggling” and “simply incredible”. In his memoir, Ford wrote bitterly about the Aipac letter signed by three-quarters of the Senate that had ruined his diplomatic plans and cast a pall on his election campaign.

Indeed, Ford lost the election to Jimmy Carter. The lobby hoped Carter, who won 71% of the Jewish vote, would abandon aspirations for a comprehensive Middle East peace, but he was quick to disappoint. The president set his sights on a peace treaty resolving the core issues of the Arab-Israeli conflict. With high poll numbers and an American public that seemed ready for a commonsense, problem-solving president, Carter voiced his belief in March 1977 in the need for a “Palestinian homeland” as a key feature of the Middle East peace he wished to achieve.

The pro-Israel lobby immediately mobilized against Carter’s peace initiative. In a closely held 50-page memorandum for the president in early June, Carter’s senior adviser on domestic political affairs warned him that he would suffer serious consequences, including risks of failing to receive the renomination of his party, as a result of lobby opposition to his public consideration of a Palestinian homeland. Undeterred, Carter offered direct criticism of what he described in an Oval Office meeting as the prime minister Yitzhak Rabin’s increasingly inflexible positions. His differences with Menachem Begin, who became Israel’s prime minister in May 1977, were even sharper. Meanwhile Carter began intensive communications with Egyptian, Syrian and Palestinian leaders.

In October 1977, the US secretary of state Cyrus Vance issued a joint communique with Soviet foreign minister Andrei Gromyko committing the superpowers to achieving “as soon as possible a just and lasting settlement of the Arab-Israeli conflict”. Though fully expecting opposition to the president’s Middle East policy, the administration was stunned by the nearly apoplectic reaction to the US-Soviet statement by both the Israeli government and the lobby. Profoundly concerned with the political damage, Carter requested a meeting with the Israeli foreign minister Moshe Dayan in New York. According to Zbigniew Brzezinski, Carter’s national security adviser, who was present at the meeting, “Dayan in effect blackmailed the President by saying that unless he had assurances that we would oppose an independent West Bank and that we would give them economic and military aid, he would have to indicate our unwillingness in his public statements here in the United States … ‘I can go,’ said Dayan, ‘to the American Jews.’” Faced with this threat, Carter surrendered.

The next day, Vance and Dayan issued a joint statement summarizing a US-Israeli “working paper” prepared in the early hours of the morning. The statement affirmed negotiations would be dramatically scaled back and would not frame a Palestinian homeland as a central issue. The end result was a celebrated “separate peace” between Israel and Egypt that earned Carter, Begin and Sadat Nobel peace prizes, but also led to the isolation of Egypt in the Arab world and the assassination of Sadat. It also set the stage for Israel’s invasion of Lebanon in 1982 and settlement projects that resulted in Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

It is likely, 13 years later, that President George HW Bush felt just as Carter must have felt when, faced with the Israel lobby’s ferocious opposition to his Arab-Israeli peace initiatives, he made public his frustration with its influence. In a failed effort to boost the prospects for the upcoming Madrid peace conference, Bush suspended US loan guarantees amounting to what Israel was spending on housing in occupied territories and faced ferocious opposition from the Israel lobby for doing so. In a press conference he described his exasperation.

“We’re up against very strong and effective, sometimes, groups that go up to [Capitol Hill]” Bush said. “I heard today there was something like a thousand lobbyists on the hill working the other side of the question. We’ve got one lonely little guy down here doing it.”

The lobby’s ability to thwart presidential peace initiatives was on particularly powerful display again during the Obama administration. No president before him had entered the White House with such detailed knowledge of the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, such a record of personal engagement with both Jews and Palestinians, and such a sustained commitment to closer American relations with Arabs and Muslims. Fully embracing a “two-state solution” to the problem, he launched a high-profile peace initiative to be jumpstarted by a full-scale Israeli freeze on West Bank settlements.

But a storm of outrage in Israel and among leaders of Israel’s lobby in the United States, and the public feud that erupted between Barack Obama and Benjamin Netanyahu, proved more costly to the former than the latter. Obama quickly reversed course, in effect replacing peace process envoy George Mitchell, who was closely identified as friendly to the Palestinians, with Dennis Ross, a lobby insider, whose advice to ditch the effort altogether the president quickly implemented. Instead of pressing Israel to stop settlements, Obama made a personal call to Mahmoud Abbas, president of the Palestinian Authority, threatening to pull $450m in American aid to the Palestinians if Abbas did not withdraw an anti-settlement resolution put forward at the UN security council. In Obama’s address to the United Nations General Assembly in the first year of his second term, he shifted dramatically from language used in his previous UN speeches. Instead of criticizing Israeli settlements and pressing for a two-state solution, he identified himself with Israeli victims of Palestinian terrorism, opposed any UN action contrary to Israel’s insistence on direct negotiations between the parties, and condemned challenges to the legitimacy of Israel as a Jewish state.

The reason for Obama’s dramatic retreat is easily inferable from his memoir, A Promised Land, in which he complains about Aipac’s ability to cow American politicians into obeisance by invoking fears of being labelled antisemitic, and emphasized his own particular vulnerability to such threats as “a Black man with a Muslim name who lived in the same neighborhood as Louis Farrakhan”.

More recently, in Joe Biden, the Israel lobby found a president who genuinely believed the Jewish state deserved the “special relationship” with the US. The firmness of that commitment was put to the test by Israel’s response to the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

Socialized into accepting the lobby’s mantra that any “daylight” between Washington and Jerusalem would encourage Arab intransigence, and remembering the political punishment Obama received for showing “tough love” to the Israelis, Biden, quashed all recommendations from his top advisers to do something meaningful to stop the Israeli onslaught on Gazan Palestinians. When he did make limited complaints about excessive civilian casualties and implemented minor delays in American resupply of Israeli armaments, the Republican Jewish Coalition responded by slamming the administration for inserting daylight into the US-Israel relationship, while Aipac sent a detailed memorandum to members of Congress defending Israeli actions as limited, necessary and designed to reduce civilian casualties.

The experience of these administrations demonstrates the wisdom and extraordinary insight of America’s first president, George Washington. In his Farewell Address, Washington warned that the American system of government could all too easily be exploited by a group with a “passionate attachment” to a foreign country. In a system designed to rely on the mobilization of countervailing power to limit the effects of factions driven by self-interest or very particular points of view, Washington argued that since any faction committed to the interests of another country would not naturally find its influence checked by effective domestic opposition, it would therefore drive the United States into exaggerated and dangerous commitments abroad and implicate it in quarrels and wars contrary to the country’s interests.

In the wake of the genocide, the politics of the issue in America have changed as numerous Americans react with passion to Israeli onslaughts in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank. Biden and Kamala Harris paid heavy costs for knuckling to Israel and its lobby. Nearly a third of voters who voted for Biden in 2020 and did not vote for Harris in 2024 said that ending Israel’s violence in Gaza was the top issue influencing their voting decisions. Across both parties, support for Israel has plummeted; sixty percent of Americans hold an unfavorable view of Israel, and a record number of Israel critics are winning congressional primaries.

But these losses have not deterred Israel or its lobby from working to reverse Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to avoid wars in the Middle East, to pursue even closer relations between the US and Israeli militaries, and to spend millions to thwart the rise of critics of the country.

To be sure, American supporters of Israel and its governments have every right to express their opinions and work to shape public policy, and the lobby is by no means the only vehicle for moneyed interests that warp American democracy. Moreover, American presidents have free will: the George W Bush administration was run by many who were in perfect ideological alignment with the Israeli right. On the other were his top foreign policy and national security officials, led by the secretary of state, George C Marshall. Their unanimous recommendation was to prevent the establishment of a Jewish state, which they believed would trigger war in the Middle East and endanger the future of US relations with the Arab and Muslim world.

news.title: This Texas coal mine will soon be home to a 1.2GW solar farm
news.text:
Construction is underway on a $1.7 billion solar and battery storage project in Texas that will turn existing coal mining land into a hub of clean energy generation.

Panamint Capital announced last week that it broke ground on the 1.2-gigawatt Big Rooter Power solar farm in Bremond, about halfway between Dallas and Houston. The project will use some of the land and assets from the adjacent Twin Oaks coal-fired power plant and Calvert surface coal mine, both of which will continue operating.

Panamint’s clean energy project will be among the largest in the nation — and, the developer claims, the biggest solar array ever built at a brownfield site in North America.

“We believe deploying new capacity at existing energy sites is the clearest way to benefit communities, ratepayers, and the environment alike,” said Apolka Totth, CEO of Panamint, a Nevada-based investment firm.

The giant installation will further boost Texas’ thriving solar sector, which this year is expected to generate more electricity than coal in the Lone Star State. The renewable resource is helping meet the state’s energy demand from data centers, manufacturing facilities, and rising air-conditioning use amid more frequent and extreme hot weather.

Panamint, which is backed by the private equity firm KKR, launched in 2019 with the goals of squeezing more life out of existing fossil-fuel infrastructure while building lower-emission facilities on the same sites. In 2023, Panamint acquired the 310-MW Twin Oaks coal plant and Calvert mine ​“with the express intention of leveraging the site’s existing characteristics to massively and rapidly expand generating capability at the lowest possible cost,” Totth said by email. 

Work has started on the first phase of the solar farm, a 491-MW section that is set to go online in August 2028. Construction will begin in December on the remaining 658 MW, which could start producing power in August 2029.

The 10,000-acre Big Rooter site will also include 1.6 gigawatt-hours of battery storage and 20 miles of new extra-high-voltage transmission lines. The investment firm says it also has the infrastructure and natural gas access needed to build at least 800 MW of gas-fired generation, either for the grid or customers like data center developers.

“Big Rooter is a landmark project that reflects the scale of investment being made in America’s energy future,” George Hershman, CEO of Solv Energy, said in a news release. The contractor is building the site’s solar array, substation, and transmission infrastructure.

Turning coal mines into clean energy 

Big Rooter’s pairing with active coal operations makes it unique within the nation’s small but growing coal-to-solar subsector, which has mainly focused on putting panels on former mine lands and retired industrial sites.

The largest of these projects is the 186-MW Tilden Solar Project in southern Illinois, followed by the 111-MW Martin County Solar Project in eastern Kentucky, which both went online last year atop abandoned coal mines.

In Louisiana, the 240-MW Dolet Hills Solar Project is now being built on a former coal mine property. And the developer BrightNight is advancing the Starfire installation on remediated mine land in Kentucky.

In 2023, when BrightNight announced the Appalachian project, electric truck startup Rivian signed on as the anchor customer, with a 100-MW power purchase agreement. Starfire was initially envisioned as a roughly 800-MW project, but is now on track for 410 MW, with construction slated for late 2027 and planned operations in 2030.

“Earlier descriptions of a larger project reflected a broader long-term vision for the site, but as development has progressed, BrightNight has focused on the configuration that best aligns with current interconnection, permitting, site, and customer considerations,” a BrightNight spokesperson said by email. ​“We remain very enthusiastic about Starfire and its importance as a major redevelopment project on former coal mining land in Eastern Kentucky.”

Repurposing old mining sites for solar power has an obvious appeal. As opposition breaks out in rural areas over using prime farmland for solar — concerns stoked by Trump administration officials, including U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins — brownfield projects allow developers to sidestep those conversations and put sullied land to use. Doing so has typically proved more complicated and expensive than placing solar panels on flat or uncontaminated fields.

The 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law and 2022’s Inflation Reduction Act provided incentives to make it easier to finance clean energy installations on mine lands, while a $500 million Department of Energy program allocated funding for projects on current or former mines.

But last year, the Trump administration and Congress added more hurdles by phasing out tax credits for solar and wind energy, effectively ending the tax bonus for brownfield developments. And the administration scrapped at least one DOE mine-land award, for Mineral Basin Solar Power, as part of its sweeping cancellation of $7.6 billion in clean energy grants in the 16 states that voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

“The federal policy landscape for developing clean energy on mines has changed, but the opportunity hasn’t,” said Jessica Wilkinson, the North America renewable energy team lead for The Nature Conservancy, a global nonprofit.

“In many parts of the country, wind and solar are the cheapest forms of energy and are succeeding on economics alone,” she added. ​“And if building on mine lands, brownfields, and landfills has fewer community conflicts, they may be seen as very enticing.” 

The nonprofit and its partners plan to develop 25 solar and battery storage projects on former mine lands that The Nature Conservancy manages in the Cumberland Forest, which spans parts of Kentucky, Tennessee, and Virginia. The first project, the 10-MW Wildcats Solar in Virginia, is expected to break ground this fall and could start delivering power to the grid next year.

Wilkinson noted that despite the federal pullback, states have continued to show support for what her group calls ​“mining the sun” projects. For example, Ohio and Colorado passed laws to incentivize renewable energy development on former industrial sites. And a handful of federal programs continue providing financial support for cleaning up coal mining areas — a crucial step for enabling future solar development.

“Communities still want to see these lands become economic engines again,” Wilkinson said.

Texas project adds solar — and more coal

Panamint, for its part, said it was able to secure clean energy incentives for Big Rooter Power before Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025, repealing large swaths of the Inflation Reduction Act.

“We ordered long-lead time equipment such as transformers and circuit breakers well before last summer’s OBBBA, so we were largely insulated from those impacts,” Totth said.

She noted that Panamint is partnering with U.S. firms First Solar and Nextpower (formerly Nextracker) to procure domestically made solar modules and racks. Big Rooter is also located in an ​“energy community” — the Department of Energy’s term for brownfield sites and areas affected by coal plant and mine closures. For those reasons, the company says it will receive a federal investment tax credit worth 50% of total project costs.

Yet as Panamint begins installing millions of solar panels in Texas, it has no plans to wind down production at the neighboring Twin Oaks coal plant.

“Twin Oaks is an economically competitive unit that provides low-cost reliability to Texas ratepayers, and we see no reason for an early retirement,” Totth said. She added that the company is also investigating both expanding the Calvert mine area and building a terminal facility to rail in coal for continued operations.

As Totth sees it, the new solar array will produce enough carbon-free power to ​“negate” the coal plant’s emissions profile on an annual basis.

It’s an example of the all-of-the-above approach to energy in Texas. Despite the massive amounts of solar, storage, and wind the state has built, it continues to cling to fossil fuels.
news.summary: Panamint Capital broke ground on a $1.7 billion solar and storage project at the Calvert coal mine. The mine and an adjacent coal plant will stay online.

news.title: Best HBCUs for Securing Top Jobs and High Salaries, Ranked
news.text:
Forbes just released its top HBCU rankings, highlighting the public and private institutions delivering the highest return on investment, graduation rates, and mid-career median pay. The recognition comes as demand for the Black college experience reaches record highs—even as campuses navigate ongoing controversies like financial aid constraints and Howard University’s recent unenrollments over unpaid balances. Despite those systemic hurdles, the culture on these campuses remains undeniably rooted in history, pride, hustle, and community. Here is a look at which schools led the ranking and what the metrics reveal about graduate outcomes.

Top Private HBCUs

1. Howard University

Despite a 2018 audit that exposed nearly $1 million in embezzled financial aid, to the historic 34-day Blackburn Center sit-in in 2021 over unlivable housing conditions and campus mold, Forbes named Howard the #1 private HBCU in the nation.

The Meeca earned the top spot based on its impressive 69% six-year graduation rate, 90% retention rate, and standout alumni including Kamala Harris, Thurgood Marshall, Toni Morrison and Taraji P. Henson. Howard graduates command an early-career median pay of $70,600, and median mid-career salaries exceeding $123,000.

2. Spelman College

Claiming the #2 spot is Spelman College, an institution founded in 1881 where sisterhood, academic prestige and global leadership shines. Spelman, the country’s first HBCU for women, boasts a 91% retention rate, a powerhouse alumni network that includes Alice Walker and Stacey Abrams, and $102,000 mid-career median pay, Forbes reported.

The Atlanta college is also known for its strong programs in biology, biochemistry, psychology, and education.

Related: The Rising HBCU Enrollment: 15 Largest Black Schools Ranked by Size

3. Morehouse College

From Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Morehouse’s pipeline of Black male talent remains unrivaled. According to Forbes, Morehouse College graduates boast a median mid-career salary of $126,700—the highest among the top three private HBCUs. 

With a roster of distinguished alumni that includes Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Spike Lee, Samuel L. Jackson, and Maynard Jackson—the first African American mayor of Atlanta—Morehouse continues to stand on a tradition of brotherhood and a century-long mandate to cultivate transformative leaders that change the world.

4. Xavier University of Louisiana

When it comes to producing Black doctors, Xavier University of Louisiana is in a league of its own. The nation’s only historically Catholic HBCU “has more Black students who go on to graduate from medical school than any other college in the country, outpacing even Ivy League campuses and huge state universities,” the school announced. 

Driven by elite programs in pre-med, pharmacy, and neuroscience, XULA turns undergraduate ambition into success well beyond the classroom with mid-career alumni salaries soaring past $104,000.

5. Hampton University

With premiere programs in journalism, business, and STEM, Hampton boasts impressive graduate outcomes with a mid-career median pay of $112,900, sending a steady pipeline of talent directly into Fortune 500 companies and top-tier law schools.

Its alumni class is equally impressive. From two-time Oscar-winning costume designer Ruth E. Carter to healthcare pioneer Dr. Sylvia Trent-Adams—the first Black nurse to serve as acting U.S. surgeon general—Hampton University consistently produces defining leaders who drive its high Forbes ranking for exceptional post-grad career success.

6. Tuskegee University

Co-founded in 1881 by Booker T. Washington, Lewis Adams, and George W. Campbell, Tuskegee University continues its storied tradition as a leader in agriculture and biotechnology. Today, it stands as the only HBCU in the country with a fully accredited College of Veterinary Medicine—producing over 75% of the nation’s Black veterinarians—and the only HBCU to offer ROTC programs for all branches of the U.S. military, including the Space Force. 

It’s the largest producer of African Americans with baccalaureate degrees in Math, Science and Engineering in Alabama, and the top producer of African American aerospace science engineers in America. Talk about impact!

7. Fisk University

Holding down the seventh spot is Nashville’s historic liberal arts school, Fisk University. Fisk continues to be a national research heavyweight, where it has historically produced more Black graduates who go on to earn PhDs in scientific disciplines than almost any other institution in the country.

National Science Foundation (NSF) data has consistently highlighted Fisk’s outsized impact in STEM fields despite its small undergraduate population of 1,015. From its legendary alumni including W.E.B. Du Bois and Ida B. Wells, to intensive undergraduate and graduate scientific training, Fisk continues to be a top launching pad for Black PhDs in physics, chemistry, and biology.

Top Public HBCUs

1. North Carolina A&T State University

The Root previously told you about NC A&T’s legendary 100-day countdown to the “Greatest Homecoming on Earth,” so it’s no surprise Forbes crowned the institution the #1 public HBCU in the nation. Based in Greensboro, NC A&T reigns supreme as the country’s largest HBCU and the single largest producer of Black engineers at both the undergraduate and graduate levels.

With civil rights leadership like the late-civil rights icon Jesse Jackson, to modern breakthroughs in aerospace and biomedical engineering and world-class STEM research, NC A&T’s graduate earning power is unbeatable.

2. Florida A&M University

Tallahassee’s own and the Sunshine State’s only public HBCU, Florida A&M University, continues to set the benchmark for academic excellence with its premiere research programs in journalism, law, and engineering. 

Beyond its legendary campus culture and high student retention rate of 88%, FAMU has become a quiet giant in healthcare, single-handedly producing 20% of the nation’s Black pharmacists. Combined with an elite alumni network that boasts groundbreaking figures like tennis pioneer Althea Gibson, Tony Award-winner Anika Noni Rose, and former mayor of Atlanta, Keisha Lance Bottoms, FAMU continuously proves that its degree hits different.

3. Prairie View A&M University

Established in 1876 as the second-oldest public university in Texas and the oldest public HBCU in Texas, Prairie View A&M University has a 74% retention rate, an early-career median pay of $72,300, and a mid-career median pay of $117,900.

Known for its elite engineering and agriculture programs, world-class nursing school, and vibrant campus culture, PVAMU shines on national rankings for high graduate earning potential, standout social mobility scores, and an unrivaled network of leaders across Texas and beyond. 

4. Morgan State University

Originally founded in 1867 as the Centenary Biblical Institute, Morgan State continues its rapid ascent toward R1 doctoral status—a prestigious designation reserved for the nation’s top-tier research universities with the highest level of research activity and grant funding.

Beyond its research momentum, Morgan State also stands out for its high-demand, cutting-edge majors, offering specialized degrees in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, applied neuroscience, and screenwriting and animation that effortlessly sets its graduates apart. The school is also a top national producer of Black engineers and STEM graduates—with nearly 17% of its alumni employed in STEM fields.

5. University of the Virgin Islands

Standing in a class of its own is the University of the Virgin Islands—the only HBCU located in a U.S. territory. Founded in 1962, UVI has become a pipeline for regional leadership and marine science research in Caribbean coral ecosystems.

The territory’s public land-grant institution has also built a strong reputation as a regional anchor across its St. Thomas and St. Croix campuses, expanding career opportunities through affordable online and on-campus degree programs. They also offer an accelerated path into medical school through Boston University, Forbes reported.

6. Tennessee State University

Nashville’s only public land-grant university serves as a major engine for workforce development. With 77 total major and degree programs and dedicated initiatives like its Pathway to Completion program—designed for non-traditional learners who have been out of school for at least two years—TSU provides accessible, career-focused degrees that yields strong returns in growing industries.

The alma mater of billionaire Oprah Winfrey is also celebrated for its SMART Tech Center that pioneers artificial intelligence coursework, and is home of one of the largest health sciences programs among HBCUs.

7. Bowie State University

Maryland’s oldest HBCU, Bowie State University, continues to punch above its weight class as a leader for STEM, computer science and cybersecurity as the seventh ranked public HBCU.

Emphasizing partnerships with federal agencies, Bowie State holds an elite designation from the National Security Agency (NSA) as a National Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense. As a result, qualified undergraduates can earn specialized Core Knowledge Units and Focus Area certificates, leading to a $100,700 mid-career median pay after graduation and high-earning, future-proof credentials.

Forbes just ranked the top 20 HBCUs that set their graduates up for success, historically educating the nation’s Black doctors, lawyers, engineers and teachers.
