news.title: Democrats Confront Their New Tea Party Reality
news.text:
Progressives appear on the verge of sweeping a trio of heavily contested Democratic primaries in Michigan and Wisconsin, alarming party operatives who fear the left-leaning candidates could endanger the party’s chances in two of the nation’s iconic swing states.

Public surveys released in recent days have pointed to significant primary leads for Assemblywoman Francesca Hong in Wisconsin’s governor’s race, for Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District and for former public health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race. 

All are set to defeat comparatively moderate opponents and will have overcome ferocious efforts by establishment-aligned forces to stop them. All have been seemingly boosted by Republicans in one way or another. All are facing some degree of worry about whether they can triumph in territory won by President Donald Trump in 2024 in November. 

All of their rises have led to finger-pointing within the party’s establishment and its moderate wing, with many arguing they were too slow to adjust to voters’ post-Biden preferences on everything from Israel to data centers to economic populism. Others are pointing to race-specific problems, with the moderate wing failing to consolidate its voters early in both the 7th District and in the Wisconsin governor’s race. 

“Shame on the establishment Democrats for not having a message that resonates with people,” said Emily Cherniack, the founder of New Politics, which is backing Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the Wisconsin governor’s race and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam in Michigan’s 7th, adding voters were looking for a different type of candidate: “People don’t want the pragmatic leader who’s going to put the country first.”

If the progressive candidates do win in November, however, they are set to provide significant boons to their movement, giving the left a counterargument to consistent doubts about their candidates’ ability to win over swing voters in the nation’s most crucial political battlegrounds.

“Michigan is ground zero for the future of the Democratic Party and a primer for the upcoming presidential race,” Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, said Friday on MSNOW. “If Abdul can win after $60 million is spent against him … that will send a signal to every other Democratic politician. If he goes on to win the general election, that sends a signal to scared electability voters.”

While progressives have often had a leg up on the Democratic establishment throughout the 2026 primary season, the potential victories for Hong, El-Sayed and Lawrence seem set to cement this year as the Democratic equivalent of the Tea Party movement that rocked the GOP in 2010. While Republicans benefited from massive political backlash to a president of the other party that year, the energy coursing through their party also resulted in the party nominating unelectable candidates in a host of critical races, allowing Democrats to maintain control of the Senate. 

Democrats, who are opening up more significant leads in public polling even as the party’s national brand remains poor, now find themselves in a nearly identical situation. President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, linked to a failed war in Iran and an inability to focus on voters’ economic concerns instead of his pet construction projects, is presenting the party with golden opportunities. The fear is the party’s primary voters will fumble them. 

There are limits to the progressive surge, which is also expected to lift Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan over Rep. Angie Craig in Minnesota’s Democratic Senate primary. House primaries between left-wing insurgents and incumbents backed by AIPAC in St. Louis and Detroit are seen as toss-ups, and most competitive seats in both House and Senate races saw establishment-backed candidates win with relatively little trouble.

The level of concern about each candidate’s ability to win in November is different: El-Sayed, a more established figure, draws the greatest electability worries from Democrats inclined to back his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, while many others note most polls of the race indicate both he and Stevens would face a tight matchup with Republican Mike Rogers. 

With the race in its final days, Stevens’ allies are still hoping a surge in Black voter turnout could lift her fortunes, though others in the party have begun to question why her campaign — and the $50 million in support from super PACs funded by the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee and others — focused so narrowly on a group which is expected to make up a quarter or less of the primary electorate.

“Having a huge lead among Black voters does make for a great tweet if you’re looking for the moral high ground,” said one Stevens-supporting Democrat in the state who requested anonymity to protect personal relationships. “But it does not matter much if you’re getting crushed with the rest of the electorate.” 

Other Democrats have long questioned the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s decision to back Stevens over state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the race last month. The committee has long said Stevens’ track record of winning a GOP-held district made her the most attractive candidate.

In Wisconsin, Hong’s membership in the Democratic Socialists of America is seen as a significant drag on her appeal, though her relatively weak opponent — Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee, is a member of the archconservative House Freedom Caucus — and focus on “permanent affordability” have convinced many Democrats in the state she can triumph regardless. 

“I’m bullish on her ability to close the deal,” said Joe Zepecki, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state. “The voters are telling us they’re looking for something different, and they think Francesca Hong is that something different.” 

Democrats in the state closely watched Hong’s appearances on Fox News and CNN on Friday, attempting to evaluate how she would stand up to relatively hostile questioning. Republicans, meanwhile, are salivating at the chance to run against her, with the Republican Governors’ Association spending millions on an ad campaign not-so-subtly intended to boost her name ID.

Wisconsin’s primary is not until Aug. 11, giving some members of the party establishment hope a last-ditch effort to convince Crowley to reenter the race with the backing of Gov. Tony Evers could still prove fruitful, especially since former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes’ exit from the contest on Thursday could help consolidate establishment support. Rep. Gwen Moore (D) endorsed Crowley on Friday morning. 

Lawrence’s candidacy has caused the most consternation. A co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, he managed to sneak up on Washington, D.C., operatives who were focused on the competition between former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink.

A focus on stopping data centers, a point of emphasis shared by Hong and El-Sayed, helped create runaway momentum for Lawrence’s candidacy. His first campaign ad featured a homeowner who feared a data center built in their town would destroy their property values. 

“People are fearful that their towns will be destroyed by these hyperscale data centers,” Lawrence told HuffPost in a phone interview on Friday. “I mean, it is an existential threat for the people who are on the front lines, and people across the district see that we have corporate-funded Democrats and corporate-funded Republicans who are united in rolling out the red carpet for these Silicon Valley billionaires to decide the future of our communities.”

Lawrence and Hong have both said their opposition to the facilities has won them the support of Trump supporters who oppose the projects, arguing it shows how economic populist issues taken up by the left can win over working-class voters who have backed Republicans in recent years. 

Moderate Democrats, however, contend their left-wing positions on other issues will ultimately matter more to those voters in November. “I think this race is 100% off the table now if Lawrence wins,”Cherniack said of the 7th District, which is expected to be one of the marquee races in the battle for the House.

In separate interviews, Maasdam and Brink both pointed to their backgrounds — he carried the “nuclear football” for former President Barack Obama, she was the first female ambassador in a war zone in American history — as key reasons for voters to back them. But both largely demurred when asked if Lawrence could win.

“Just looking at the Republican ads, they want to run against William Lawrence and it’s for a good reason,” Maasdam said. 

“It’s a purple district,” Brink said.

However, the two candidates — whose surrogates have traded words over the past week about whether either candidate is a “spoiler” for the other – were much harsher on each other than on the progressive frontrunner.

“There are more non-Will voters than there are Will voters,” Maasdam said when asked if Brink should drop out of the race. “I hate to see that bloc split. It’s a tough decision for Bridget.”

Brink was unsparing in her criticism of Maasdam: “Matt has spent his entire campaign being dishonest to voters,” she said. “He’s been lying about me, smearing my record. He’s been hiding the truth about his Republican past, and his campaign is being propped up by more than $5 million in dark money super PAC ads from the data center industry.”

Cherniack said Democrats are ultimately working off a hangover caused by President Joe Biden’s political downfall and former Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss, causing the party’s voters to look anywhere else. She compared it to her own dating life, noting that after breaking up with a technology company vice president, she proceeded to date a man with no checking account and a motorcycle.

“Democrats had been told and forced to vote for these ‘sensible’ candidates,” she said. “Primary voters are in a rebound era.”

A focus on stopping data centers, a point of emphasis shared by Hong and El-Sayed, helped create runaway momentum for Lawrence’s candidacy. His first campaign ad featured a homeowner who feared a data center built in their town would destroy their property values. 

“People are fearful that their towns will be destroyed by these hyperscale data centers,” Lawrence told HuffPost in a phone interview on Friday. “I mean, it is an existential threat for the people who are on the front lines, and people across the district see that we have corporate-funded Democrats and corporate-funded Republicans who are united in rolling out the red carpet for these Silicon Valley billionaires to decide the future of our communities.”

Lawrence and Hong have both said their opposition to the facilities has won them the support of Trump supporters who oppose the projects, arguing it shows how economic populist issues taken up by the left can win over working-class voters who have backed Republicans in recent years. 

Moderate Democrats, however, contend their left-wing positions on other issues will ultimately matter more to those voters in November. “I think this race is 100% off the table now if Lawrence wins,”Cherniack said of the 7th District, which is expected to be one of the marquee races in the battle for the House.

In separate interviews, Maasdam and Brink both pointed to their backgrounds — he carried the “nuclear football” for former President Barack Obama, she was the first female ambassador in a war zone in American history — as key reasons for voters to back them. But both largely demurred when asked if Lawrence could win.

“Just looking at the Republican ads, they want to run against William Lawrence and it’s for a good reason,” Maasdam said. 

“It’s a purple district,” Brink said.

However, the two candidates — whose surrogates have traded words over the past week about whether either candidate is a “spoiler” for the other – were much harsher on each other than on the progressive frontrunner.

“There are more non-Will voters than there are Will voters,” Maasdam said when asked if Brink should drop out of the race. “I hate to see that bloc split. It’s a tough decision for Bridget.”

Brink was unsparing in her criticism of Maasdam: “Matt has spent his entire campaign being dishonest to voters,” she said. “He’s been lying about me, smearing my record. He’s been hiding the truth about his Republican past, and his campaign is being propped up by more than $5 million in dark money super PAC ads from the data center industry.”

Cherniack said Democrats are ultimately working off a hangover caused by President Joe Biden’s political downfall and former Vice President Kamala Harris’ loss, causing the party’s voters to look anywhere else. She compared it to her own dating life, noting that after breaking up with a technology company vice president, she proceeded to date a man with no checking account and a motorcycle.

“Democrats had been told and forced to vote for these ‘sensible’ candidates,” she said. “Primary voters are in a rebound era.”

news.title: Democrats Confront Their New Tea Party Reality

news.title: It's been a summer of bad news for Mayor Bass. Can she reset the narrative?
news.text: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass was riding relatively high two months ago, weathering pitched challenges from Spencer Pratt on the right and Nithya Raman on the left to emerge as the top vote-getter in the city’s June 2 mayoral primary. "Tomorrow begins the second half of this journey," an ebullient Bass told supporters at the Line Hotel in Koreatown on election night. There’s been a lot less to cheer about lately. Bass' summer has been beset by a string of negative news. Staff members on both her campaign and administration teams have left. She was away from the city — just as she was at the start of the devastating 2025 firestorms — when a blaze ignited at the Lineage cold-storage food warehouse in Boyle Heights, inundating the heavily Latino surrounding neighborhoods with noxious fumes. And that was all before the release of a new report showing that homelessness in the city rose for the first time in three years, undercutting a pillar of Bass’ fall runoff campaign against Raman. "In terms of policy, politics and operations, I don't know if there has been a single piece of good news that has come out of her camp since the primary," said Dan Schnur, a professor of political communications at USC, UC Berkeley and Pepperdine. “Bass’ only possible path to reelection at this point is raising so much money that Raman simply can’t be heard," Schnur said. With three months to go in the campaign, Schnur and other analysts say Bass has time to turn things around. Nonetheless, they say, the summer of bad news will force Bass to reset her campaign narrative — including shoring up her support with Eastside Latinos in the wake of the Lineage fire. Bass carried 35 Latino-majority neighborhoods in the June 2 election, including Boyle Heights, compared to seven for Raman and just one for Pratt. Yet when she attended a community meeting in early July in the wake of the Lineage fire, she was met with boos from the largely Latino crowd. "The Lineage fire has deeply eroded the Latino support she was getting from the eastern side of the city, which she needed to build towards November. That’s going to be a real challenge for her now," said Sara Sadhwani, a professor of politics at Pomona College. Bass was in Chicago at the dedication of the Barack Obama Presidential Center when the fire broke out and returned to Los Angeles the next evening as the fire continued to burn, casting a black plume of smoke over the neighborhood and leaving a stench for weeks as food rotted in the burnt building. The episode was a stark reminder that Bass was abroad on a diplomatic trip in Ghana at the start of the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles in January 2025. High winds and elevated fire risk were forecast as she departed for Africa. "It reinforces the narrative of the Palisades, her being out of town," said Fernando Guerra, a professor of political science and Chicana/o Latina/o studies at Loyola Marymount University. At a news conference Friday, Bass ordered city agencies to delay the processing of rebuilding permits for the Lineage burned-out cold-storage warehouse in Boyle Heights until regulators have found ways to subject the project to strict environmental review. “They shouldn’t even think about rebuilding until they’ve cleaned up the mess they’ve created,” Bass told reporters. The harsh line Bass is taking against Lineage, however, comes after disclosures that one of her former top advisors, Yusef Robb, had taken on a role doing crisis communications for highly scrutinized company. Robb spent the first half of the year working for Bass as an unpaid spokesperson, delivering statements for the mayor on some of the most controversial issues she faced, including allegations that she watered down an after-action report on the Palisades fire. After the mayoral primary, Robb transitioned to a role as an unpaid, unofficial advisor to the mayor, her office said. He took on a role with Lineage on June 19. The roles overlapped, but Robb and the mayor's office insisted there was a firewall between Robb and the mayor regarding the Lineage fire. Robb has since said he would no longer advise the mayor. Bass also took heat for comments she made that the air surrounding the burned-out warehouse wasn’t dangerous to breathe, despite some residents reporting feeling sick from the smoke. Bass spokesperson Ilanna Morales said the mayor was simply stating what public health officials had determined, which was that conditions didn’t warrant a mandatory evacuation. "Any assertion that the Mayor does not think smoke is dangerous is distorting her remarks and taking them out of context," said Morales. Morales also noted that the mayor’s response to the fire included opening mobile health clinics throughout Boyle Heights, providing respiratory health screenings and oxygen level checks. Councilmember Monica Rodriguez, who has endorsed the mayor, said that Bass has done a good job related to the Lineage fire, but that critics are piling on to a politician in a susceptible position. "We live in a day and age where you see someone vulnerable, and everyone attacks and pounces," Rodriguez said. "Everyone is angry, and they want to blame someone." The mayor’s team is also pushing back on assertions that it’s been a summer of unrelenting bad news, touting among other things the recent World Cup soccer matches at Inglewood’s SoFi Stadium as a major success that boosted L.A. businesses, hotels and Metro ridership. Bass supporters pointed to her second appointment as chair of L.A. Metro along with her announcement that she wants to make buses and trains free, as well as her administration's role in helping broker new ownership for the downtown "Graffiti Towers" that would begin immediate abatement of the tagging on the buildings. "The last few weeks have been challenging; no mayor is perfect," said Nella McOsker, who runs the downtown business group Central City Assn. and has endorsed the mayor. "I think that Bass has a relentless desire to respond, engage and correct in the midst of these crises." One of those crises is the city’s chronic problem with the homeless population. Throughout her reelection campaign, Bass has repeatedly touted two straight years of decreases in homelessness from 2024 to 2025 as one of her main arguments for why she should be given another four years by Angelenos. But 2026 ended that positive run. The city's unsheltered homeless population went up 7.9% this year, according to a report by the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Bass cited cuts at the state and federal level as partially responsible for the increase, saying that Trump administration actions have led to higher gas, groceries and rent prices, which has driven some Angelenos to the edge of homelessness. Bass continued to site a "historic decline" in homelessness since she took office — an 11% drop overall since 2023. But the uptick citywide this year contrasted sharply with Raman's district, where homelessness actually decreased by 49%. The discrepancy gave Raman an outlet to attack the mayor while touting her own record on homelessness in her district. "This is a moral outrage and it is a failure. The approach to homelessness that Mayor Bass has led and defended brought us here," Raman said at a press conference the day the numbers were released. The mayor has argued that her own program, Inside Safe, was at least partially responsible for the drop in Raman's district and also argued that Raman's role as chair of the Housing and Homelessness Committee on the Council makes her responsible for citywide homelessness numbers as well. "The homeless count is as much an indictment of Nithya Raman as it is of Karen Bass. If you're going to blame one you have to blame them both," said Rodriguez, who sits on the Housing and Homelessness Committee in Council. Bass is gearing up for the fall campaign with a new campaign team, led by Julie Chávez Rodríguez. Chávez Rodríguez, a granddaughter of disgraced labor leader Cesar Chavez, was campaign manager for President Biden’s aborted 2024 re-election campaign, and then took the same role for Vice President Kamala Harris after Biden dropped out. "She’s getting Graffiti Towers cleaned up, announced a fare-free Metro, hosted a successful World Cup, and more," said Chávez Rodríguez. "Those are big wins that Angelenos see and feel, it’s not campaign rhetoric. The Mayor’s getting things done across the City and that’s how you win.” Chávez Rodríguez came on after the mayor's previous top campaign strategist, Douglas Herman, left the campaign a week after the Boyle Heights fire began, citing "strategic differences" for his departure. Along with Herman, media consultant Larry Grisolano and research director Mike Rice also left. Bass' director of communications at City Hall, Kolby Lee, also resigned this summer, the latest in a string of Bass' communications staff to leave her office over the past nine months. Bass did significantly outraise Raman in the first campaign finance cycle of the general election, which her campaign said showed the mayor's momentum and support in the city. Bass raised more than $510,000 in June, while Raman took in just over $170,000. Political consultant Mike Trujillo, who is supporting Bass, said the kinds of turbulence Bass has faced this year is par for the course for a big-city mayor. "Stuff happens; things are always moving," Trujillo said. "Bad things are always happening, and good things are always happening."
news.summary: The Lineage cold-storage fire, the rise in homelessness numbers and staff turnover have created new challenges for Bass as she heads to a Nov. 3 runoff with Nithya Raman.
news.author: Noah Goldberg

news.title: Barabak: Democrats are at each other's throats — this time over the 2028 calendar
news.text: Come 2028, the Democratic presidential campaign promises to be a banger, with all sorts of intrigue and subplots layered within a wide-open fight for the nomination. There’s the prospect of same-state rivals going at it. (California’s Gavin Newsom vs. Kamala Harris; Georgia’s Sen. Jon Ossoff vs. Sen. Raphael Warnock.) There’s sure to be a generational divide, a split over how much time and energy Democrats should spend rehashing the Trump era, and, inevitably, a clash between standard-bearers of the left, the far left and the party’s increasingly small center-left. All that remains in the offing, however, as none of the major prospects have formally declared their candidacies. Political tradition, and self-preservation, require waiting at least until after November's midterm election to jump into the race. In the meantime, Democrats have seemingly resolved at least one 2028 fight, a fracas marked by snarking, backbiting and plenty of acrimony — all the things that make our politics such a grand and glorious endeavor. We speak of the contest to determine which state will hold the first vote of the 2028 nominating process. And the winner is … South Carolina! This was a blow to Nevada, the runner-up in the calendar sweepstakes, and not a very sporting one at that. The state Democratic Party issued a huffy news release, insisting Nevada will be the candidates’ first true test of 2028 — emphasis added — reprising the argument over which state offers the best starting path to reclaim the White House and, thus, deserves the coveted lead voting slot. (California, a perennially frustrated onlooker, is not set to vote until March 7, several weeks into the balloting, which is supposed to start Jan. 22.) For decades, the political calendar was unchanged and, mostly, unchallenged. Iowa went first, holding its quaint and quirky precinct caucuses — neighbors gathered in church halls, school libraries and the like as they worked through arcane rules involving "realignment" and "viability thresholds" — followed by New Hampshire's first-in-the-nation primary. In 2024, President Biden shook things up. He'd failed miserably in Iowa in his runs for president, so Biden had no problem slotting South Carolina first after the state resurrected his lifeless 2020 candidacy. (Iowa didn't help itself by making a thorough mess of its 2020 caucuses, taking nearly a month to certify a winner.) The change set off a free-for-all this time around, as a dozen states bid for the chance to vote first. (The two major political parties set the rules for choosing their presidential nominees, independent of one another. Republicans are expected to stick to the traditional lineup, starting with the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire primary, followed by contests in Nevada and South Carolina.) Last month, after nearly a year of consideration, the Democratic Party's Rules and Bylaws Committee voted for six states to hold their contests in a window between late January and the end of February. They are, in order, South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia. The lineup will be presented to the full Democratic National Committee to be voted on and finalized later this month. Doubtless, you — a normal person — have paid little or no attention to any of this. You've got more important things to do, like binge-watching "Widow's Bay," or not melting. But party leaders and political insiders take the process extremely seriously. At stake: bragging rights, a modest economic boost and the chance for local analysts and office-holders to make frequent appearances as experts on the cable-TV chat shows. The jostling grew particularly fierce between South Carolina and Nevada. More than 50% of the Democratic primary electorate in South Carolina is Black. In Nevada, Latinos are a substantial and increasingly powerful voting bloc. So, naturally, the competition between the two states assumed fraught racial overtones, which is unfortunate but not surprising, given Democrats' penchant for picking at sore spots and turning on each other at the slightest provocation. It was also rather pointless. The order of the presidential calendar is consequential, but far from determinative. South Carolina was vital to Biden's success. But so, too, was the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, which sharply curtailed the Democratic nominating fight. Barack Obama's 2008 victory in Iowa gave him a huge lift, but he lost to Hillary Clinton the following week in New Hampshire and had to fight another six months before winning the nomination. Presidential campaigns have changed drastically in the 50 years since a little-known Jimmy Carter quietly burrowed into Iowa, spent months bunking in folks' extra bedrooms, then burst to national fame by outperforming his more prominent rivals. Today, the race is a 24/7 affair, followed by voters in all 50 states. While local concerns may come up here and there — the proposed Yucca Mountain nuclear waste dump in Nevada, beach erosion in South Carolina's Lowcountry — the same issues and controversies confront candidates and animate the contest regardless of whether a field of soybeans, a white church steeple or a Southern fish fry serves as the backdrop. Obviously, the voting has to begin somewhere and the competition between states is well and good. But the trash-talking and, especially, antagonism over race and ethnicity is gratuitous and needlessly divisive. Candidates will show they have the stuff to win the nomination, or not, by building their best case and pitching it to voters. No matter if it's a Black church in Las Vegas or a Latino neighborhood in North Charleston. Any location will do.
news.summary: The choice of which state begins the presidential balloting turned into a needlessly divisive conflict over race and ethnicity. Nevada didn't take South Carolina's selection well.
news.author: Mark Z. Barabak

news.title: El-Sayed vs. Stevens: How the Michigan Primary Could Reshape Democrats
news.text: Michigan Democrats head to the polls Tuesday in what has become one of the party's most closely watched primaries of the year, not simply because it will decide who succeeds retiring Senator Gary Peters, but because many Democrats see it as a referendum on the party's future. Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and Representative Haley Stevens are competing for the Democratic nomination in a race that has grown into a national proxy battle over ideology, campaign spending, and influence within the party. Stevens has emerged as the establishment favorite, backed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer and supported by tens of millions of dollars in outside spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee's affiliated super PAC. El-Sayed, meanwhile, has rallied the progressive wing of the party, earning endorsements from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez while arguing that grassroots organizing can overcome institutional power. The outcome could reverberate far beyond Michigan. If El-Sayed wins both the primary and the general election against Republican Mike Rogers, progressives will point to the victory as evidence that their message can prevail in one of the country's most competitive battleground states. If he secures the nomination but loses in November, moderates are likely to argue the opposite—that progressive candidates remain a liability in swing-state elections. Stevens faces the same test in reverse, with supporters arguing she represents Democrats' strongest chance of keeping the seat in party hands. Money, Influence and the AIPAC Debate Much of the national attention surrounding the race has centered on the unprecedented level of outside spending. United Democracy Project, AIPAC's affiliated super PAC, has poured roughly $30 million into supporting Stevens and opposing El-Sayed, according to the Associated Press, making it the organization's largest investment in a single race to date. For progressives, the spending has transformed Michigan into a broader fight over whether outside money can determine Democratic primaries. Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution, the organization that grew out of Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign, said a Stevens defeat would send a message well beyond the state's borders. "This election is ultimately a test of whether unlimited outside spending can substitute for genuine grassroots organizing," Geevarghese told Newsweek. "Regardless of where the money comes from, voters are demonstrating that there are limits to what money alone can buy." He argued the contest is ultimately about more than AIPAC itself, saying Democratic voters are responding to candidates focused on affordability, housing and health care. "We've been outspent," Geevarghese said. "We have not been out-organized." Stevens' campaign rejects the notion that outside spending explains her position in the race. Campaign spokeswoman Joetta Appiah told Newsweek that polling has consistently shown Stevens as the strongest Democrat to face Rogers and argued Republicans privately would prefer to run against El-Sayed instead. Democratic strategist Doug Gordon said an El-Sayed victory would nevertheless be interpreted as a setback for AIPAC regardless of what happens in November. "There is no question that an El-Sayed victory would be a huge defeat for AIPAC and another sign of how toxic their brand has become within Democratic politics," Gordon told Newsweek. He also noted Michigan's unusually late primary calendar leaves the eventual nominee with fewer than 100 days to unify Democrats before the general election against Rogers—a challenge for either campaign. Jim Kessler, Third Way's executive vice president for policy, said the AIPAC spending fight obscures a demographic reality specific to the state. Michigan has a higher percentage of Arab American residents than any other state in the country, he said, while its Jewish population is less than half the size of its Arab American population. "Israel will continue to be a dividing line in Democratic politics," Kessler told Newsweek. "That will be the case no matter who wins next Tuesday." Michigan's Democratic establishment has largely lined up behind Stevens. Whitmer endorsed her last week, calling the congresswoman someone who has "what it takes to win." The endorsement also revived memories of Whitmer's decisive victory over El-Sayed in the party's 2018 gubernatorial primary. El-Sayed's campaign dismissed the move as further evidence that the "corporate establishment has closed ranks," arguing voters—not party leaders—will ultimately decide the nominee. The Fight for Black Voters Whether either campaign can build a winning coalition may ultimately depend on Black voters, who make up roughly one-fifth of Michigan's Democratic primary electorate. Historically, Black voters have tended to support more moderate candidates in high-profile Democratic primaries, including former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton over Sanders in Michigan in 2016. Recent polling suggests Stevens continues to hold an advantage among Black voters overall, particularly those over 55, while El-Sayed has found stronger support among younger and college-educated voters across racial lines. Both campaigns have spent the closing weeks focused heavily on that constituency. Stevens has made repeated visits to Detroit and Flint. El-Sayed has campaigned in Pontiac while visiting Black churches and community events across southeast Michigan. Still, El-Sayed continues to face questions over his prominent role in the 2024 "uncommitted" movement, which encouraged Democrats to withhold presidential primary votes in protest of the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza. More than 100,000 Michigan Democrats ultimately cast uncommitted ballots that year, and CNN interviews with Black voters and party leaders found some remain skeptical of El-Sayed because of his involvement. Matt Bennett, co-founder of the centrist think tank Third Way, has been among his sharpest critics, calling El-Sayed "a radical" and predicting Stevens would perform better against Rogers in November. “It’s pretty evident that running far to the left is extremely dangerous in a place like Michigan,” Bennett told The Hill. National Ambitions Under the Microscope As the race has tightened, Stevens and her allies have increasingly questioned whether El-Sayed is focused on Michigan—or on building a broader national movement. Those attacks intensified after leaked audio from a Zoom donor call, first published by Politico's Playbook, captured El-Sayed describing a Senate victory as an opportunity to reshape the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 election cycle and potentially support a primary challenge to Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman. "You put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed said, describing the broader political implications of his campaign. His campaign later told Politico that he had been speaking metaphorically and argued Fetterman has too often aligned himself with the Trump administration. Stevens has seized on the comments, portraying El-Sayed as more interested in becoming a national political figure than representing Michigan in the Senate. During the campaign's final debate, she described him as a "celebrity candidate." Stevens campaign spokesman Arik Wolk pushed back on that framing directly, saying her focus is entirely on the state. "Haley fights for Michigan and only Michigan," Wolk told Newsweek. "In the Senate, she'll fight for all Michiganders from every zip code to lower costs, protect manufacturing jobs, and take on Donald Trump's corruption and abuses of power. And as Michigan's most effective fighter, she's got a plan to deliver for all of Michigan on day one: stop Trump's tariffs on groceries, win back our supply chain from China, and stop utility companies from jacking up rates on Michigan families." Momentum Appears to Shift The competing strategies appear to have reshaped the race in its closing days. While earlier surveys showed Stevens narrowly ahead or the contest effectively tied, recent public polling has consistently given El-Sayed the advantage. A SoCal Strategies survey conducted July 28-30 found him leading 56 percent to 39 percent. An Emerson College Polling survey for WLNS-TV and WOOD-TV released the same day showed a 57-41 lead, while a Tavern Research poll first reported by Politico put El-Sayed ahead 48-37. Just weeks earlier, polling conducted by The Detroit News and WDIV-TV had shown Stevens with a narrow edge, prompting pollster Richard Czuba to describe the race as "wide open" because of the large number of undecided voters. Prediction markets have shifted alongside the polls. By Thursday morning, Kalshi gave El-Sayed an implied 84 percent chance of winning the Democratic nomination, up sharply from 64 percent just days earlier. Polymarket showed an even larger advantage, pricing his chances at roughly 91 percent. Whitt Kilburn, a political science professor at Grand Valley State University, said Michigan's electorate has become unusually difficult to predict. "Regarding the conventional wisdom on Michigan voters, all bets are off," Kilburn told Newsweek, pointing to education, race, gender, ideology and attitudes toward Israel and U.S. foreign policy as factors reshaping turnout. The Road to November Whoever wins Tuesday will immediately face another difficult challenge. Michigan has been one of the nation's closest battleground states in recent elections. Donald Trump carried the state in 2024 with 49.7 percent of the vote to Kamala Harris' 48.3 percent after Joe Biden won it in 2020. Trump also narrowly carried Michigan in 2016, the same year Sanders stunned Clinton in the Democratic presidential primary. Rogers also demonstrated Republicans' competitiveness last cycle, losing to Elissa Slotkin by less than a percentage point. Kilburn said this year's political environment could prove somewhat more favorable for Democrats because some swing voters who backed Trump in 2024 may be less likely to participate without the former president on the ballot. Kessler cautioned against reading too much into a primary win alone. The primary electorate and the general electorate are not the same voters, he said, and El-Sayed would still need to win over the decisive middle in a swing state even amid what looks like a favorable environment for Democrats in November. Head-to-head polling suggests either Democrat would begin the general election within striking distance. A late-June Quantus Insights survey gave Stevens a 1.4-point advantage over Rogers and El-Sayed a 1.1-point edge, with both matchups well within the margin of error. Republicans have not won a Michigan Senate seat since 2001, but the contest remains one of the party's strongest pickup opportunities as they look to expand their Senate majority. Tuesday's primary will answer one immediate question: who Democrats believe is best positioned to defend one of the country's most competitive Senate seats. The broader debate over whether the party's future belongs to its establishment or to the progressive movement challenging it is likely to continue long after Michigan's votes are counted. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate primary has become a battle over more than a nomination.

news.title: Trump’s Approval Rating Is Underwater in 11 States He Won Comfortably
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating is underwater in at least 11 states that he carried by double digits in the 2024 election, a sign of growing dissatisfaction with the president’s performance ahead of November’s midterms even in places where support for him is strongest. Nationally, the president is at 36 percent approval and 59 percent disapproval as of July 30, leaving him significantly underwater with a net approval rating of -24, according to Civiqs’ rolling online tracking poll of registered voters. The poll has garnered more than 120,000 responses since January 20, 2025, when Trump returned to office for a second term. While Trump’s approval rating is highest in the most reliably Republican states, the state-by-state breakdown shows it is underwater in 11 states that he carried by at least 10 points in the 2024 presidential election against Democratic former Vice President Kamala Harris. The decline in approval ratings in those states could be consequential. Small shifts in voter sentiment could have an outsized impact on November’s midterm elections, when control of Congress is at stake, and Republicans are fighting to preserve their narrow majorities in the House and Senate for the remainder of Trump’s second term. Trump's Approval Slips in States He Easily Carried Trump's approval rating was positive in every state he won in 2024 by at least 10 percentage points when he was inaugurated for a second term in January 2025, but it has since slipped underwater in at least 11 of those states. He has had a net negative approval rating in some of those states since he announced tariffs on U.S. trading partners in April last year. In other states, including Kentucky and Missouri, Trump's approval rating went underwater after he announced a war with Iran in February. The Civiqs poll shows him with a net negative approval rating in 11 of those states that he carried by double digits in the 2024 election. They are: But even in the states where Trump’s approval rating is currently highest, the latest data still shows a clear decline from the start of his second term. He began his second term with +45 net approval in Wyoming and +31 in North Dakota, but that has now slipped to +19 in both states. Use the map below to explore where Trump’s net approval rating stands in each state: Important Races to Watch Democrats need to pick up four seats in November to take control of the Senate, making competitive races in Iowa, Ohio and Texas particularly critical. In Iowa, Democratic state Representative Josh Turek is in a tight race against Republican U.S. Representative Ashley Hinson for a seat that the GOP considers pivotal for preserving the party’s Senate majority. In Ohio, Democrats are counting on former Senator Sherrod Brown to unseat Republican incumbent Jon Husted. And in Texas, Democratic state Representative James Talarico is facing Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, in one of the country’s most closely watched Senate races. All three are states that Trump comfortably carried in 2024, but where his approval rating is now underwater. Key Battleground States Trump remains underwater in all seven of the swing states that he carried in the 2024 presidential election. His approval rating continuing to decline in those states could hurt Republicans in November’s midterm elections, and allow Democrats to pick up key seats in the House and Senate. What the White House Says The White House has repeatedly dismissed the president’s low approval ratings, pointing to Trump’s 2024 election victory as the clearest measure of public support. In response to inquiries about polling, White House spokesman Davis Ingle previously told Newsweek that the Americans who voted for Trump gave him a mandate to “deliver on his popular and commonsense agenda.” Trump “has already made historic progress not only in America but around the world. It is not surprising that President Trump remains the most dominant figure in American politics,” Ingle said. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Sam Wilson.

news.title: This is what democracy looks like to Maine Democrats? | Opinion
news.text:
Jacob Posik is the political director of Maine Civic Action and the director of legislative affairs of Maine Policy Institute.

There are landslides, there are blowouts and there are coronations.

On July 25, the Maine Democratic Party officially crowned former Senate President Troy Jackson as its nominee for the United States Senate. Jackson captured 566 of 571 delegate votes at the party’s emergency nominating convention, replacing Graham Platner after Platner’s spectacular political collapse. 

The margin wasn’t surprising. By the time delegates arrived in Bangor, the outcome had long been decided. The convention was simply the final act in a process that had already delivered Jackson the nomination before most Democrats even realized a contest was — allegedly — taking place. 

The irony is hard to ignore. 

The party that lectures us about “defending democracy” ultimately entrusted one of the most consequential decisions in Maine politics to 571 insiders after more than 216,000 Mainers participated in the June Democratic primary. 

Just 0.26% of the people who cast ballots for a Democrat in June were empowered to determine who would challenge Sen. Susan Collins in November. 

To be fair, the Maine Democratic Party was operating under extraordinary circumstances. Replacing a nominee after a primary is exceedingly rare. But the party effectively had every legal right to establish whatever replacement process it wanted.

Ultimately, Maine Democrats opted for a system where delegate selection became the election. Once the deck was stacked internally in Jackson’s favor, the convention in Bangor became a formality. 

Other candidates might have mounted serious campaigns if more than 571 people were allowed to take part in the decision. Does this sound familiar? It should. 

Just two years ago, Democrats nationally found themselves in a similar predicament.

Former President Joe Biden’s disastrous debate performance crystallized concerns that had been building for months. His cognitive decline could no longer be dismissed. Polling showed Donald Trump would handily defeat him. Eventually, Biden did what many believed he should have done much sooner by withdrawing from the race.

At that point, Biden’s decision wasn’t controversial. But what happened next certainly was. 

Rather than opening the nomination to a robust competition among the Democratic Party’s brightest leaders, party elites moved with breathtaking speed to consolidate behind Vice President Kamala Harris. A virtual roll call of party delegates quickly ratified the predetermined outcome. 

No meaningful debates. No open contest. No opportunity for Democratic voters to evaluate competing visions for the future of their party.

The machine had spoken.

Maine Democrats just followed that same blueprint.

My understanding of democracy has always been that political power flowed upward from voters, not downward from party leadership. Yet rank-and-file Democrats continue to watch from the sidelines while a small handful of insiders determine who carries their banner. 

To be clear, this critique of the process is not meant to be an indictment of Jackson, necessarily. Perhaps he would have won in a statewide primary. But considering he barely beat Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and finished behind Dr. Nirav Shah in the Democratic gubernatorial primary — two candidates who also vied to replace Platner — it’s certainly not a given. 

Sadly, we’ll never know the answer because Democratic voters weren’t given the chance to decide.

When the judgment of 571 Mainers substitutes for the judgment of more than 216,000, something fundamentally undemocratic has occurred, even if everyone ultimately agrees with the result. 

Democrats constantly warn us that democracy is under threat. They speak passionately about protecting institutions, expanding voter participation and ensuring every voice is heard.

Those are admirable principles. But they lose their meaning when party brass repeatedly illustrates that those principles mean nothing.

When internal party decisions repeatedly bypass or exclude the will of ordinary voters — through lightning-fast virtual roll calls or insider delegate conventions — the message becomes clear: In the Democratic Party, only a select few closest to the levers of power make decisions for everyone else.

When push comes to shove, this is how both the national and Maine Democratic parties operate. 

Maine Democrats have every reason to be frustrated. Not because Jackson is the nominee, but because so few had the opportunity to decide whether he should be. Perhaps they should even fear Jackson will face a similar fate as Kamala Harris because of this process. 

Call this nomination efficient, practical or even necessary under extraordinary circumstances. 

But don’t call it democracy. That’s not what democracy looks like.
news.summary: You can call the process to nominate Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate efficient, practical, even necessary. Just don't call it fair to voters.
news.author: Jacob Posik

news.title: Did Tucker Carlson Just Host the First Meeting of 'The Lincoln Project 2.0'?
news.text:
If you have ever watched Tucker Carlson’s podcast after he was shown the door at Fox News, the room in the photo might look familiar to you. It’s the dining area of Carlson’s Maine cabin, a room where he’s conducted the majority of his interviews for the podcast.

Greene posted the photo on the X platform, and then conservative influencer Shawn Farash came up with what I think was the best take in a sea of pretty hilarious takes.

Ladies and gentlemen I present to you:The Lincoln Project 2.0 pic.twitter.com/XmdVfAaMQJ— Shawn Farash (@Shawn_Farash) August 1, 2026

Most people had fun either coming up with AI-generated memes that feature the photo, or just coming up with names for the group.

All of the main players in this photo have one thing in common: they shot themselves in the foot with President Donald Trump after previously winning his trust, and then alienating him in various ways. And each decided that if you’re going to get on Trump’s bad side, you may as well go after him with everything you’ve got.

What they’ve already demonstrated is that whatever they’ve got isn’t enough. It’s not enough to salvage whatever future they may have in conservative media or conservative politics. Not only did they alienate Trump, but they discredited themselves as conservatives. In the process, they put a huge amount of distance between themselves and most people on the right.

Most conservatives see these people and their takeaway is, “If he’ll promote himself as Trump’s best friend for so long and then turn on him like this, what kind of person is he anyway?” The question is rhetorical, because to even ask this, your mind is already made up. The person in question is a two-faced, backstabbing, disingenuous narcissist. Or something like that.

While I wasn’t pondering any meme or caption ideas, I was curious about what kind of critical mass this group is seeking to form. What do they hope to accomplish?

I’m not even going to entertain conspiracy theorists who’ve speculated that the flow of money into some of their own or their spouses’ bank accounts would make for some interesting reporting. I’ll let some intrepid investigative reporter dig into that one.

What I will ponder, strictly for entertainment purposes, is whether this group is following The Lincoln Project’s (TLP's) playbook. Is this The Lincoln Project 2.0?

At least one or two of the people in this photo know, even with the healthy egos they possess, that they could never start another political party. They have to know the Democrats really won’t have them, and the Libertarians, well, they’re Libertarians.

Meanwhile, the communists over at the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) might find a use for them, but only during the infatuation phase. Anyone who’s anyone knows that with a socialist or a communist, nothing lasts – not the relationship, not the money, not the property, not the food, not the peace.

Would this group of grifters be looking to start a super PAC just like those other former Republicans who formed TLP in 2019? Or are they just a bunch of noisemakers looking for a way to stay relevant by making more noise and taking selfies?

TLP’s primary goal was to defeat Trump in the 2020 election by trying to drive a wedge between Trump and his conservative base. That didn’t happen. What did happen was a pandemic, changed election procedures, mail-in voting, ballot harvesting, and Joe Biden getting 81 million “votes” – that’s 11 million more than Barack Obama got in 2008, and six million more than Kamala Harris got in 2024. It would appear that Democrats are doing much better with voters who are dead in recent years.

So, I wouldn’t put too much stock in the effectiveness of TLP in taking Trump out in 2020. If TLP accomplished anything it was to give its principals a steady income without forcing them to go out and get a real job. They were able to make money bashing Trump, someone who made clear to them that he had no use for them. They included George Conway, Steve Schmidt, John Weaver, and Rick Wilson, among others.

That group had previously supported such conservative stalwarts as George H.W. Bush, John McCain, John Kasich, and Arnold Schwarzenegger. With resumes like theirs, it’s a wonder why Trump didn’t want them on his team.

That group of losers built TLP’s platform on themes that accused Trump of working against the rule of law, the Constitution, and traditional American values.

With a platform like that, it was a little awkward – OK, a lot awkward – when it was discovered that roughly 21 men accused Weaver of doing some things that went against traditional American values.

Axios reported in January 2021, “During the past week, several men have alleged on social media that Weaver sent them unsolicited and sexually suggestive messages, sometimes coupled with offers of employment or political advancement.”

Weaver then sent a statement to Axios that said, “To the men I made uncomfortable through my messages that I viewed as consensual mutual conversations at the time: I am truly sorry. They were inappropriate and it was because of my failings that this discomfort was brought on you.”

In terms of output, TLP was able to produce campaign-style ads attacking Trump and his administration. The group endorsed Joe Biden for president, and of course, they raised tens of millions of dollars, which is what super PACs do.

By March 2021, the New York Times, once an ally of TLP’s in the campaign to attack Trump and put Biden in the Oval Office, realized it no longer needed those former “conservatives.” And so, it did what leftists always do: it turned on them.

Under the headline, “Inside the Lincoln Project’s secrets, side deals and scandals,” the team-written article chronicled the ways in which TLP’s leaders enriched themselves and it dug into the Weaver story.

Is this the roadmap for anti-Trump success? Maybe. It’s just not clear who the constituency is for this.

While the never-Trump movement has recently added Carlson, Greene, Kent, and Massie to its ranks, overall the movement is one where relevancy has gone to die.

To be honest, I really can’t figure out what this group is hoping to accomplish. My sense is that a super PAC would involve far too much commitment for a group known mostly for its lack of commitment. At the same time, looking around that table, I’m sure none of them much trust each other, knowing that each has already demonstrated their own lack of trustworthiness on a grand scale.

So, what would you yourself call this group? Your guess is as good as mine.

news.title: Michael Goodwin: Fauci’s refusal to answer questions at Senate hearing reveals important truth
news.text:
Because Dr. Anthony Fauci repeatedly cited the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering any questions, last week’s Senate hearing was reduced to a grudge match that produced no new information on the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic that killed more than 7 million people worldwide, including 1.1 million Americans.

Fauci was the nation’s most important health official and White House adviser as the virus gained a foothold in early 2020 and proceeded to spread its death grip across all 50 states.

Despite his infuriating refusal to even defend himself, lest his answers lead to criminal charges, the hearing still served a useful purpose, albeit on a separate crucial matter.

Only because of the persistence of GOP Sen. Rand Paul, chair of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which released much of those diaries, do we know that Fauci often said in private things that contradicted what he said publicly.

A key example involves suspicions that a leak from a lab in China that was doing gain-of-function research, funded in part by America, was the source of the virus. 

Fauci was well aware of the funding and the lab’s work, but nonetheless denounced the suspicions, calling them conspiracy theories.

Yet he privately conceded he was uncertain, especially after a conference call with 11 other scientists, most of whom thought the lab-leak theory was the most likely culprit, a fact he noted in his diary but not publicly.

Similarly, he boasted in his diary that he was a principal architect behind the idea of shutting down much of society, including schools, offices and even churches. 

In a March 15, 2020, entry, under the words “BIG DAY!” in red letters, he wrote that he had a conversation with then Gotham Mayor Bill de Blasio and “convinced him based on what I was saying publicly and my conversation tonight to close the NYC schools.”

He cited “a similar call” with an aide to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who told him that based on Fauci’s public remarks, Newsom “decided to close the schools in California as well as the bars and restaurants.”

Although those policies lacked a factual basis, they caused long-term damage to children’s learning and resulted in draconian economic pain now widely regarded as unnecessary.

“They always come back and say, ‘Fauci was responsible for shutting schools down.’ I had nothing to do [with it]!” he claimed.

Star-struck

Fame also warped his judgment. 

As he told his Dear Diary after a worshipful piece on the front page of the Washington Post: “It is not hyperbole to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable in the world.”

He also was star-struck, noting that Barbra Streisand called him asking for vaccine advice.

CNN’s Jake Tapper, for example, twice hosted dinners at his home for Fauci, while others texted and emailed him with praise for his public appearances and private conversations.

They supposedly were covering the death and destruction, what the origins were and what the government was doing to stop it.

But the media didn’t cite their favorite source’s double talk or private misgivings. 

Instead of covering Fauci, they were covering for Fauci, and once again betrayed the public by hiding an inconvenient truth.

The case fits an infuriating pattern seen repeatedly since Donald Trump entered the political arena in 2015.

After the networks and major publishing outlets decided he was unfit for the Oval Office, they distorted their coverage to damage him and boost his opponents.

Still no final verdict

In this case, Fauci was the good guy of the pandemic and Trump the nutty, erratic problem, facts be damned.

The pattern was established during 2016 general election campaign, when the media gleefully swallowed hook, line and sinker Hillary Clinton’s fake Russian dossier.

Leaks from the FBI, the Obama White House and CIA created a feverish race to confirm that Trump was a Kremlin asset. 

It was a dirty trick in which the deep state nearly stole an election, yet the same media that turned it into Pulitzer gold never owned up to their mistakes.

Another example of malfeasance is the way legacy organizations showed no curiosity about Joe Biden’s cognitive decline in the White House, despite numerous public examples. 

He gave almost no interviews, and was protected by his staff from answering even routine questions, lest he misstate a policy that would have to walk back.

The media could see all this, but never dared to dig into his health if it would help Trump.

It was not until Biden’s brain freeze in the first debate in 2024 that left-leaning outlets panicked that Trump would win again. 

When Kamala Harris got the nomination in a backroom deal, there were no demands for a clean, open process.

There was only applause for the “joy” that Harris brought to the race.

Fauci benefited from the same double standard, for the same reason. 

Anyone who made Trump look bad was a hero.

The first COVID cases in the US were discovered in January 2020, the start of Trump’s final year in the Oval Office in his first term.

According to his diary, Fauci wrote in the same month about the possibility that “the virus might have originated in an open-air ‘wet market,’ ” where live animals were sold, in Wuhan, China.

He also wrote that “we know the market was not the source, it was the amplifier,” and added, that, “Having said that, somewhere the virus jumped from animals to humans.”

A rival theory about a leak from a Wuhan lab also gained traction, and as Trump began calling it the “China virus,” the usual media suspects revolted.

A New York Times reporter wrote on social media that “Someday we will stop talking about the lab leak theory and maybe even admit its racist roots.”

But six years later, with Fauci getting a sweeping pardon from Biden, there is still no final COVID verdict in sight.

As Dr. Scott Atlas, a Fauci critic and member of the White House Coronavirus Task Force, writes in The Post: “the media clung to an absurd, Kafkaesque hero-worship of the man who was destroying millions of lives.”

news.title: Cyberattacks Threaten Water Supplies Across Country. Tim Walz Or Iran May Be To Blame Depending On Who You Ask.
news.text:
As recent cyberattack incidents threaten water supply systems across multiple states, some officials are saying Iran may be to blame while President Donald Trump is pointing a finger at a state run by a former Democratic rival.

The water supplies of at least seven states, including Minnesota and Michigan, have been targeted by these largely unprecedented attacks as of Saturday, The New York Times reported. Anonymous officials cited by the outlet said it is likely, but not yet certain, that Iran — which the U.S. is currently at war with — was responsible for the cyberattacks. Trump, however, hinted at there being another possible culprit during a cabinet meeting Friday at Camp David.

“I blame it on Minnesota because they are grossly incompetent,” Trump said at the meeting, Politico reported. He went on to call the blue state’s Democratic Gov. Tim Walz “corrupt.”

“Iran has bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota,” the president added, according to the outlet. “I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack. I think Minnesota ought to get its act together.”

At the time, Minnesota was the only state identified to have been targeted in the attacks. Michigan was confirmed to have been targeted as well the following day, The New York Times reported. The other five states considered to also be targets have not yet been named as of Saturday afternoon. 

As of yet, none of the targeted states’ water supplies were altered to become harmful to drink, the outlet reported.

Walz responded to Trump’s apparent insinuation that his administration was to blame for the cyberattacks, writing in a Friday X post that the president “knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too.” (RELATED: Is Involvement In The War With Iran In America’s Best Interest? A Daily Caller News Foundation Debate)

Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too.This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran. https://t.co/e70UpK65P6— Governor Tim Walz (@GovTimWalz) July 31, 2026

“This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran,” the governor added.An AP-NORC survey conducted from July 23–27 found that 64% of U.S. adults, including 68% of independents and 37% of Republicans, believed the Trump administration’s war in Iran was not “worth fighting.” Eighteen U.S. service members have been killed in the war as of Saturday afternoon.

Anonymous officials told the outlet Saturday that, while the investigation into the origins of the cyberattacks was not yet conclusive and lacked forensic proof, Iran is the most likely perpetrator, as the Middle Eastern nation has gone after similar water systems in the past.

The mayor of a small Minnesota city affected by the attacks likewise told the outlet he is “getting bits and pieces of information from the state of Minnesota.” While the FBI reportedly “are pretty sure it’s Iranian actors,” the mayor claims, they are reluctant to state this publicly.

“The FBI is aware of recent public reporting around Water and Wastewater (WWS) sectors,” a spokesperson for the Bureau told the Daily Caller News Foundation in a statement. “The FBI and our interagency partners are fully engaged to protect critical infrastructure and we remain well-equipped to protect against cyber threats of all varieties.”

news.title: AOC’s Low Favorability Complicates Democrats’ Push for Change: Poll
news.text: A new national poll reveals that while a majority of Democrats are eager for sweeping changes within their party, high-profile progressive leader Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez faces low favorability ratings that could complicate her emergence as a unifying national figure. The CNN/SSRS survey, which was conducted between July 23-27, found that a majority of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents favor significant changes to the party's leadership and strategic direction. At the same time, the poll registered a 26 percent national favorability rating for Ocasio-Cortez, one of the party’s most prominent progressive voices. Her unfavorable rating was at 36 percent. Among adults ages 18 to 34—a demographic frequently viewed as a core source of support for the New York Democrat—her favorability stood at 28 percent. The congresswoman's favorability went up to 30 percent among those aged 35 to 49. The poll surveyed 1,225 respondents, with the margin of error being +/-3.2 at the 95 percent confidence level. The findings underscore a complex strategic dilemma for Democrats as they grapple with their future. While rank-and-file voters express widespread dissatisfaction with current leadership, the data indicates that high visibility has not yet translated into broad national appeal for one of the party's most prominent alternatives. Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly stated she is not running for president in 2028, though she remains a leading voice in the party's progressive wing and a prolific national fundraiser. Newsweek has reached out to Ocasio-Cortez's office and the Democratic National Committee for comment via email and contact form respectively. news.title: Iran suspected in cyberattack on US water systems across at least seven states
news.text: A cyberattack has affected water systems in at least seven U.S. states, and the full scope of the damage may be larger, The New York Times reported. Minnesota was the first state to disclose incidents involving its water infrastructure, followed by Michigan. No formal federal announcement has identified the attacker, but Iran has emerged as the leading suspect in the preliminary investigation. The FBI and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday that water systems in at least seven states had reported incidents to federal authorities. Officials said there was no indication that drinking-water supplies had been contaminated or disrupted. Utilities across the country were nevertheless preparing for possible failures in the computer systems used to monitor water quality and chemical levels. American officials described the scale of the attack as unprecedented. Iran, however, has previously been linked to attempts to compromise water infrastructure abroad. In 2020, ynet reported that Iran had carried out a cyberattack against Israeli water facilities. A Western intelligence official later told the Financial Times that the operation was intended to increase chlorine levels in water supplied to Israeli homes. Four Israeli officials and one Western official said at the time that the attackers had penetrated software controlling Israeli water pumps after routing their activity through American and European servers to conceal the code’s origin. According to the Western official, the attack could have caused the pumps to shut down once abnormal chemical readings were detected. That could have left thousands of Israelis without running water during a heat wave. U.S. authorities have not concluded that the latest attack was directed by Iran. Officials emphasized that the investigation remains in its early stages and that cyber investigations can take months before firm conclusions are reached. The New York Times reported that Iran has intensified cyber activity against American targets since the war involving Israel and the United States began. Iranian hackers have also previously attempted to target similar water facilities in the U.S. The newspaper said the incidents did not appear to be financially motivated, reducing the likelihood that ordinary cybercriminals were responsible. President Donald Trump played down the reports Friday and questioned whether Iran had carried out the attack. “I think Minnesota is behind it,” Trump said. “I don’t believe there was an Iranian cyberattack.” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who served as Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris’ running mate in the most recent election, rejected Trump’s remarks. “This is what modern warfare looks like,” Walz said. After Trump spoke, federal officials said privately that Iran remained the main suspect, though they stressed that investigators had not yet obtained conclusive evidence. Nate George, mayor of Braham, a small city north of Minneapolis reportedly targeted in the operation, told The New York Times that local and federal authorities had little doubt about who was responsible. “We are getting bits and pieces of information from the state of Minnesota and the FBI,” he said. George, a Republican running for Minnesota state auditor, said authorities were “pretty confident” that Iranian actors were behind the attack but were reluctant to say so publicly. Federal officials declined to identify all the affected states. Michigan, however, confirmed that several communities had reported incidents resembling those described by federal agencies. “We have received a small number of reports from communities in Michigan indicating activity consistent with what federal agencies have described,” state spokesperson Dale George said. He added that all affected systems continued to operate safely and that there were “no known impacts posing a public-health concern.” Alex Orleans, a former U.S. government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, said Tehran has carried out a wide range of operations against American, Israeli and other Middle Eastern targets since the war began. The intrusion into American water systems appeared to mark a major escalation, he said. “What is unprecedented here is that we are seeing direct, tangible effects on control systems inside critical U.S. infrastructure,” Orleans told The New York Times. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Friday that hackers had targeted “water facilities of all sizes.” It advised operators to disconnect potentially vulnerable controllers from the internet. The attack had resulted in boil-water notices and the continued manual operation of some systems, the agency said. Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said the hackers most likely exploited available vulnerabilities rather than selecting particular cities for strategic reasons. The reports come amid growing tensions in the Middle East and speculation that military operations against Iran could soon resume. CBS reported Saturday that an Israeli official said Israel was unaware of any decision to fully renew the military campaign and had not been asked to participate in military action against Iran. Israel has maintained public silence while waiting for a decision from the White House and seeking to avoid being portrayed as pressing for a wider war. American embassies across the region, including in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Israel, have issued security warnings urging U.S. citizens to leave or prepare for immediate departure in the event of further escalation.
news.summary: The FBI and environmental regulators are investigating incidents affecting facilities of different sizes, while officials say water supplies remain safe and caution that no definitive attribution has been made

news.title: Trump’s legal crusade against news media falters
news.text: NEW YORK — Donald Trump’s early legal wins against broadcasters ABC and CBS have given way to defeats and retreats as courts and newsrooms act to protect press freedom.“News organizations recognize that the only positive outcome to this is prevailing against the president and standing up for the reporters and their newsrooms,” said Ken Paulson, director of the Free Speech Center at Middle Tennessee State University.At the end of July, the Justice Department withdrew subpoenas issued to New York Times journalists who had written articles about the security of Trump’s presidential aircraft.It was forced to act after a federal judge slammed the administration’s sloppy legal work and found it violated protections granted to journalists and their sources.The president has also filed defamation suits targeting The New York Times over articles and a book about the origins of his fortune, and the Wall Street Journal over an article about a salacious letter he sent to Jeffrey Epstein. Both are floundering.“If you’re willing to stand up to Trump, you’re going to do fairly well in court, given the lack of merit behind the cases that he has filed,” observes Dan Kennedy, a journalism professor at Northeastern University in Massachusetts.The cases involving ABC and CBS ended in December 2024 and July 2025, with the broadcasters promising to pay $15 million and $16 million, respectively.Trump sued ABC for defamation over statements about a civil judgment against Trump in a sexual assault case. He took CBS to court for allegedly misleading viewers by airing different clips of the same answer from an interview with 2024 Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris.But most legal experts agree that the courts could have thrown out Trump’s claims.Both reached the settlements “for business reasons,” said Kennedy.CBS’s parent company Paramount Global, for instance, was seeking regulatory approval for its merger with Skydance.Media strategyAfter ABC kept talk-show host Jimmy Kimmel, a nightly critic of Trump, on the air, and elected not to air a live Trump speech about supposed electoral fraud, the network now faces threats to some of its local station licenses from federal authorities.In another case, the BBC, which the US president is suing for $10 billion over an allegedly misleading edit of one of his speeches, has adopted a strategy that experts expect to become more widespread.The British broadcaster is demanding that Trump’s legal team produce financial documents in order to quantify the damages suffered.“That is the biggest deterrent of all for a man who has constantly resisted efforts to look inside his empire and financial circumstances,” said Paulson.Trump’s real objective, however, is not to win the lawsuits, experts say.“You go right back to the beginning of his political career, 11-12 years ago, and it’s been a central part of his strategy to discredit the news media,” said Kennedy.“He does that by insulting them, calling them fake news, calling them enemies of the people, and he does it by filing lawsuits.”Paulson said that “Trump and his lawyers have no realistic expectation that they will prevail in a court of law somewhere down the road.”“But that can take years and millions of dollars, and Trump knows from his business experience that if he can apply enough pressure, someone will cough up a check.”
